name_of_work: Work without Hope by Samuel Taylor Coleridge
content: All Nature seems at work. Slugs leave their lair-- The bees are stirring--birds are on the wing-- And Winter slumbering in the open air, Wears on his smiling face a dream of Spring! And I the while, the sole unbusy thing, Nor honey make, nor pair, nor build, nor sing. Yet well I ken the banks where amaranths blow, Have traced the fount whence streams of nectar flow. Bloom, O ye amaranths! bloom for whom ye may, For me ye bloom not! Glide, rich streams, away! With lips unbrightened, wreathless brow, I stroll: And would you learn the spells that drowse my soul? Work without Hope draws nectar in a sieve, And Hope without an object cannot live.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved strawberries very much. One day, Lily went to the store with her mom and saw a great big box of strawberries. She asked her mom if they could buy them, and her mom said yes.

When they got home, Lily decided to make a strawberry smoothie. She put some strawberries in the blender and added some milk. Then she turned on the blender and watched as the strawberries changed into a yummy pink drink.

Lily was so happy with her great strawberry smoothie that she drank it all up. From that day on, Lily knew that she could change strawberries into something even more delicious.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. They see a big round thing that can spin. They want to try it.

"Can we go on the spinny thing?" Anna asks Ben.

"Yes, let's go!" Ben says. They run to the spinny thing and climb on. They hold on tight and push with their feet. The spinny thing goes faster and faster. They feel the wind on their faces and laugh.

"Wow, this is fun!" Anna says.

"I like it too!" Ben says.

They spin for a long time. Then they feel dizzy and stop. They get off the spinny thing and sit on the grass. They close their eyes and wait for the dizziness to go away.

"Are you okay?" Anna asks Ben.

"I'm okay, just a little dizzy," Ben says.

"Me too," Anna says.

They open their eyes and look at each other. They smile.

"That was a good spin," Ben says.

"Yes, it was," Anna says.

They lie down on the grass and relax. They feel the sun on their skin and the breeze on their hair. They feel happy and safe.

"Can I give you a massage?" Anna asks Ben.

"A massage? What is that?" Ben asks.

"It's when you rub someone's back or shoulders or head to make them feel good," Anna says.

"Okay, you can try," Ben says.

Anna moves closer to Ben and puts her hands on his back. She rubs gently and makes circles with her fingers. She moves up to his shoulders and then to his head. She massages his hair and ears.

"How does that feel?" Anna asks Ben.

"It feels nice," Ben says. "You are a good friend, Anna."

"Thank you, Ben. You are a good friend too," Anna says.

They hug each other and smile. They feel happy and safe. They like to play in the park. They like to spin and massage. They are friends.

name_of_work: To an army wife, in Sardis by Sappho
content: To an army wife, in Sardis: Some say a cavalry corps, some infantry, some, again, will maintain that the swift oars of our fleet are the finest sight on dark earth; but I say that whatever one loves, is. This is easily proved: did not Helen--she who had scanned the flower of the world's manhood-- choose as first among men one who laid Troy's honor in ruin? warped to his will, forgetting love due her own blood, her own child, she wandered far with him. So Anactoria, although you being far away forget us, the dear sound of your footstep and light glancing in your eyes would move me more than glitter of Lydian horse or armored tread of mainland infantry

name_of_work: Artist's Life by Ella Wheeler Wilcox
content: Of all the waltzes the great Strauss wrote, Mad with melody, rhythm--rife From the very first to the final note, Give me his "Artist's Life"! It stirs my blood to my finger ends, Thrills me and fills me with vague unrest, And all that is sweetest and saddest blends Together within my breast. It brings back that night in the dim arcade, In love's sweet morning and life's best prime, When the great brass orchestra played and played, And set our thoughts to rhyme. It brings back that Winter of mad delights, Of leaping pulses and tripping feet, And those languid moon-washed Summer nights When we heard the band in the street. It brings back rapture and glee and glow, It brings back passion and pain and strife, And so of all the waltzes I know, Give me the "Artist's Life." For it is so full of the dear old time-- So full of the dear friends I knew. And under its rhythm, and lilt, and rhyme, I am always finding--you.

Once there was a girl who wanted to swim. She was very obedient and had brought a folder with her to the beach. She couldn't wait to jump into the ocean and have some fun.

When she got there, she put on her swimming suit and grabbed her folder. Then she ran to the water. She laughed and yelled as she splashed around in the warm, blue waves. 

After swimming for a while, the girl got tired and went back to the beach. She carefully dried off and changed back into her clothes. Then she put her folder into her bag and headed home. 

The girl was so happy that she had obeyed her parents and gone swimming. She knew it was a great way to have fun and stay healthy. She couldn't wait to come back and swim again!

Once upon a time, there was a family who had a special dish. It smelt so delicious that it made everyone in town very envious. Every day, the family would settle down to eat the dish. All the family members always enjoyed the dish. One day, the family decided to share their dish with the people in town. So they put it in the middle of the town square. Everyone gathered around the dish and settled down to enjoy it. It was so delicious that everyone wanted to have it. Everyone was happy and settled down to eat the dish together. The end.

The young boy marched through the forest with his flashlight. He seemed so brave to the creatures of the forest, and they all watched him march.

The young boy found a lake. He bent down and looked into the lake. The little boy was surprised to see a frog. It was smiling up at him!

The boy pointed his flashlight at the frog and said: "Hello frog! What are you doing here?"

The frog smiled and said: "I'm just enjoying the moonlight. Would you like to join me?"

The young boy smiled and said: "Yes! I'd love to join you!" So the young boy and the frog enjoyed the moonlight together. The forest creatures watched them and smiled.

Once upon a time, there was a bunny named Hop. He lived in a big thick forest, and he loved to jump around and explore. But when winter came, the forest got cold and dark. All of the leaves on the trees turned black and blew away.

But still, Hop loved to hop around, even when it was cold and dark. He hopped up and down the hills, looking for something new to explore. He hopped through the trees, over logs, and around the streams.

Suddenly, one cold and dark winter day, Hop spotted something new. He hopped over to find a big, black bird. The bird was singing so quietly, it almost seemed like winter didn't exist. Hop hopped closer and watched the bird for a moment, before moving on.

He hopped around for the rest of the day, exploring all the new places the winter brought. He saw some foxes and rabbits, and the stars came out in the night. Hop had a wonderful time, despite the cold and darkness of winter.

name_of_work: Bees, So Many Bees by Anna Jackson
content: After twenty years of marriage, we walked out of the bush and on to a rough dirt road we followed till we saw a pond we might be able to get to. The ground was boggy and buzzing. The pond was thick with weed and slime. It was not the sort of pond anyone would swim in, but we did -- picking and sliding into the water over the bog and bees, bees we suddenly noticed were everywhere, were settling on our hair as we swam, ducks turning surprised eyes our way. After twenty years of marriage what is surprising isn't really so much the person you are with but to find yourselves so out of place in this scene, cold but not able to get out without stepping over bees, so many bees.

name_of_work: Mad Girl's Love Song by Sylvia Plath
content: I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead; I lift my lids and all is born again. (I think I made you up inside my head.) The stars go waltzing out in blue and red, And arbitrary blackness gallops in: I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead. I dreamed that you bewitched me into bed And sung me moon-struck, kissed me quite insane. (I think I made you up inside my head.) God topples from the sky, hell's fires fade: Exit seraphim and Satan's men: I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead. I fancied you'd return the way you said, But I grow old and I forget your name. (I think I made you up inside my head.) I should have loved a thunderbird instead; At least when spring comes they roar back again. I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead. (I think I made you up inside my head.)

name_of_work: The force that through the green fuse drives the flower by Dylan Thomas
content: The force that through the green fuse drives the flower Drives my green age; that blasts the roots of trees Is my destroyer. And I am dumb to tell the crooked rose My youth is bent by the same wintry fever. The force that drives the water through the rocks Drives my red blood; that dries the mouthing streams Turns mine to wax. And I am dumb to mouth unto my veins How at the mountain spring the same mouth sucks. The hand that whirls the water in the pool Stirs the quicksand; that ropes the blowing wind Hauls my shroud sail. And I am dumb to tell the hanging man How of my clay is made the hangman's lime. The lips of time leech to the fountain head; Love drips and gathers, but the fallen blood Shall calm her sores. And I am dumb to tell a weather's wind How time has ticked a heaven round the stars. And I am dumb to tell the lover's tomb How at my sheet goes the same crooked worm.

Once upon a time there was a girl named Jane. She was three years old and loved to play with her dolls. One day while she was playing, she had an idea. She wanted to make a new dress for one of her dolls.

So Jane found some pretty cloth and began to measure it. But then something awful happened! She accidentally cut it too short.

Jane was so sorry. She tried her best to fix it, but she couldn't. She started to cry.

But then her mom came over and said, "Don't worry, Jane. We can just measure some more cloth and try again."

And so Jane measured some new cloth and made a beautiful dress for her doll. She was so happy!

The end.

Once upon a time, there were two friends. They were good friends and liked to play together. One day, they decided to do something special to make their house cleaner. They went to the closet and got a big mask. They wore it and began to clean the house.

They scrubbed the floor and washed the windows. They picked up all the toys and swept the cobwebs away. They even dust the walls and vacuumed the stairs. Everything looked so clean and good.

When they were done, they felt so pleased with themselves. They hugged each other and high fived. They had done a great job of cleaning. Then they removed their masks and went outside to play together.

name_of_work: Sad and Alone by Maurice Manning
content: Well, this is nothing new, nothing to rattle the rafters in the noggin, this moment of remembering and its kissing cousin the waking dream. I wonder if I'll remember it? I've had a vision of a woman reclining underneath a tree: she's about half naked and little by little I'm sprinkling her burial mounds with grass. This is the kind of work I like. It lets me remember, and so I do. I remember the time I laid my homemade banjo in the fire and let it burn. There was nothing else to burn and the house was cold; the cigar box curled inside the flames. But the burst of heat was over soon, and once the little roar was done, I could hear the raindrops plopping up the buckets and kettles, scattered out like little ponds around the room. It was night and I was a boy, alone and left to listen to that old music. I liked it. I've liked it ever since. I loved the helpless people I loved. That's what a little boy will do, but a grown man will turn it all to sadness and let it soak his heart until he wrings it out and dreams about another kind of love, some afternoon beneath a tree. Burial mounds--that's hilarious.

One sunny day, a little girl named Lily went to the park with her mom. They sat down on a bench and shared some grapes. "Mommy, can we drive to the store and get more grapes?" asked Lily. "Sure, we can go for a drive and get some more grapes," replied her mom.

So, they got into their car and drove to the store. They found some really juicy grapes that were rich in flavor. "These grapes are so yummy!" said Lily. "Yes, they are very delicious," agreed her mom.

On the way back home, they saw a big truck driving on the road. "Look, Mommy! That truck is so big!" exclaimed Lily. "Yes, it is a very big truck," said her mom. When they got home, they enjoyed their grapes and talked about their fun drive to the store.

name_of_work: As I Walked Out One Evening by W.H. Auden
content: As I walked out one evening, Walking down Bristol Street, The crowds upon the pavement Were fields of harvest wheat. And down by the brimming river I heard a lover sing Under an arch of the railway: 'Love has no ending. 'I'll love you, dear, I'll love you Till China and Africa meet, And the river jumps over the mountain And the salmon sing in the street, 'I'll love you till the ocean Is folded and hung up to dry And the seven stars go squawking Like geese about the sky. 'The years shall run like rabbits, For in my arms I hold The Flower of the Ages, And the first love of the world.' But all the clocks in the city Began to whirr and chime: 'O let not Time deceive you, You cannot conquer Time. 'In the burrows of the Nightmare Where Justice naked is, Time watches from the shadow And coughs when you would kiss. 'In headaches and in worry Vaguely life leaks away, And Time will have his fancy To-morrow or to-day. 'Into many a green valley Drifts the appalling snow; Time breaks the threaded dances And the diver's brilliant bow. 'O plunge your hands in water, Plunge them in up to the wrist; Stare, stare in the basin And wonder what you've missed. 'The glacier knocks in the cupboard, The desert sighs in the bed, And the crack in the tea-cup opens A lane to the land of the dead. 'Where the beggars raffle the banknotes And the Giant is enchanting to Jack, And the Lily-white Boy is a Roarer, And Jill goes down on her back. 'O look, look in the mirror, O look in your distress: Life remains a blessing Although you cannot bless. 'O stand, stand at the window As the tears scald and start; You shall love your crooked neighbour With your crooked heart.' It was late, late in the evening, The lovers they were gone; The clocks had ceased their chiming, And the deep river ran on.

name_of_work: The Listeners by Walter de la Mare
content: 'Is there anybody there?' said the Traveller, Knocking on the moonlit door; And his horse in the silence champed the grasses Of the forest's ferny floor: And a bird flew up out of the turret, Above the Traveller's head: And he smote upon the door again a second time; 'Is there anybody there?' he said. But no one descended to the Traveller; No head from the leaf-fringed sill Leaned over and looked into his grey eyes, Where he stood perplexed and still. But only a host of phantom listeners That dwelt in the lone house then Stood listening in the quiet of the moonlight To that voice from the world of men: Stood thronging the faint moonbeams on the dark stair, That goes down to the empty hall, Hearkening in an air stirred and shaken By the lonely Traveller's call. And he felt in his heart their strangeness, Their stillness answering his cry, While his horse moved, cropping the dark turf, 'Neath the starred and leafy sky; For he suddenly smote on the door, even Louder, and lifted his head:-- 'Tell them I came, and no one answered, That I kept my word,' he said. Never the least stir made the listeners, Though every word he spake Fell echoing through the shadowiness of the still house From the one man left awake: Ay, they heard his foot upon the stirrup, And the sound of iron on stone, And how the silence surged softly backward, When the plunging hoofs were gone.

name_of_work: Washington's Monument, February, 1885 by Walt Whitman
content: Ah, not this marble, dead and cold: Far from its base and shaft expanding--the round zones circling, comprehending, Thou, Washington, art all the world's, the continents' entire--not yours alone, America, Europe's as well, in every part, castle of lord or laborer's cot, Or frozen North, or sultry South--the African's--the Arab's in his tent, Old Asia's there with venerable smile, seated amid her ruins; (Greets the antique the hero new? 'tis but the same--the heir legitimate, continued ever, The indomitable heart and arm--proofs of the never-broken line, Courage, alertness, patience, faith, the same--e'en in defeat defeated not, the same:) Wherever sails a ship, or house is built on land, or day or night, Through teeming cities' streets, indoors or out, factories or farms, Now, or to come, or past--where patriot wills existed or exist, Wherever Freedom, pois'd by Toleration, sway'd by Law, Stands or is rising thy true monument.

name_of_work: On Being Human by C.S. Lewis
content: Angelic minds, they say, by simple intelligence Behold the Forms of nature. They discern Unerringly the Archtypes, all the verities Which mortals lack or indirectly learn. Transparent in primordial truth, unvarying, Pure Earthness and right Stonehood from their clear, High eminence are seen; unveiled, the seminal Huge Principles appear. The Tree-ness of the tree they know-the meaning of Arboreal life, how from earth's salty lap The solar beam uplifts it; all the holiness Enacted by leaves' fall and rising sap; But never an angel knows the knife-edged severance Of sun from shadow where the trees begin, The blessed cool at every pore caressing us --An angel has no skin. They see the Form of Air; but mortals breathing it Drink the whole summer down into the breast. The lavish pinks, the field new-mown, the ravishing Sea-smells, the wood-fire smoke that whispers Rest. The tremor on the rippled pool of memory That from each smell in widening circles goes, The pleasure and the pang --can angels measure it? An angel has no nose. The nourishing of life, and how it flourishes On death, and why, they utterly know; but not The hill-born, earthy spring, the dark cold bilberries. The ripe peach from the southern wall still hot Full-bellied tankards foamy-topped, the delicate Half-lyric lamb, a new loaf's billowy curves, Nor porridge, nor the tingling taste of oranges. --An angel has no nerves. Far richer they! I know the senses' witchery Guards us like air, from heavens too big to see; Imminent death to man that barb'd sublimity And dazzling edge of beauty unsheathed would be. Yet here, within this tiny, charmed interior, This parlour of the brain, their Maker shares With living men some secrets in a privacy Forever ours, not theirs.

Once upon a time there was a poor, old lady who lived in a tiny shack. She was very lonely, for she had no family or friends to talk to. One day the old lady was outside her shack, crying and weeping. She was feeling so lonely and sad. 

Suddenly, a rich man with a long pole was walking by. He saw the old, poor lady weeping and said, "Hey little lady, why are you so sad?" 

The old lady told the man her story and he was filled with sadness. He could not leave her alone, so he gave her the pole that he was holding. The old lady was so thankful but did not know why he had done this kindness.

The man replied, â€œMy pole can help you make money. Use it to make a fishing net and you can use it to catch fish. That way you can sell the fish and make some money.â€ The old lady was so filled with joy and happiness. 

The old lady was thankful for the man's kindness and began using the pole to make fishing nets. She was soon able to make enough money to fill her shack with food and smiles. 

The story of the kind rich man and the old, poor lady teaches us that kindness and generosity are some of the most powerful things in the world. We should never forget to show kindness and compassion to all those in need.

name_of_work: We Were Simply Talking by Andrew Hudgins
content: We were simply talking, probably work, or relatives or even Christmas presents, when the car slid and I corrected, fishtailed and I corrected, then we were gone, sliding sideways, sliding backward on black ice and staring into the grill of a diesel tractor, also sliding, and in that instant I was ready to die. I saw my wife and was overjoyed that I had married her, though our marriage was already falling apart, and I loved the car, a brown Toyota, loved being warm in the car while it was white, cold, bitter out in the world we'd lost control of. I loved every molecule of breath I wasn't taking, and for the moment I forgave myself every sin and failure of my life, including this ridiculous and undignified early death. The car snapped backward into a frozen ditch. I sat speechless, shaking, my wife speechless also, and a man pulled up, a salesman: You folks okay? Suddenly the car radio roared, and by the car a dog barked wildly and, yes, we were fine. Fine. We were fine. But what was "fine," I wondered, and why do we always, always have to speak?

Lily and Ben were camping with their mom and dad in the woods. They had a big tent where they slept at night. They liked to explore the trees and the flowers and the animals during the day.

One day, they saw a small bird with a broken wing on the ground. It looked sad and scared. Lily and Ben wanted to help the bird. They ran to their mom and dad and told them what they saw.

"Mom, dad, there is a bird that is suffering. It has a bad wing and it cannot fly. Can we help it?" Lily asked.

"Let's go and see, but we have to be very gentle and careful. The bird might be afraid of us," dad said.

They followed Lily and Ben to where the bird was. Mom took a soft cloth and wrapped it around the bird. She lifted it up and held it close to her chest. The bird made a quiet sound.

"Shh, it's okay, little bird. We are not going to hurt you. We are going to take you to our tent and make you feel better," mom said.

Lily and Ben smiled. They walked with mom and dad to their tent. They made a cozy nest for the bird with some leaves and grass. They gave it some water and seeds. The bird ate and drank and looked more calm.

"Thank you for helping the bird, mom and dad. You are very kind," Lily said.

"Yes, thank you. Maybe the bird will get better soon and fly again," Ben said.

They watched the bird for a while. Then they cuddled with mom and dad in their sleeping bags. They fell asleep, dreaming of the bird and the woods.

name_of_work: For My Lover Returning to His Wife by Anne Sexton
content: She is all there. She was melted carefully down for you and cast up from your childhood, cast up from your one hundred favorite aggies. She has always been there, my darling. She is, in fact, exquisite. Fireworks in the dull middle of February and as real as a cast-iron pot. Let's face it, I have been momentary. A luxury. A bright red sloop in the harbor. My hair rising like smoke from the car window. Littleneck clams out of season. She is more than that. She is your have to have, has grown you your practical your tropical growth. This is not an experiment. She is all harmony. She sees to oars and oarlocks for the dinghy, has placed wild flowers at the window at breakfast, sat by the potter's wheel at midday, set forth three children under the moon, three cherubs drawn by Michelangelo, done this with her legs spread out in the terrible months in the chapel. If you glance up, the children are there like delicate balloons resting on the ceiling. She has also carried each one down the hall after supper, their heads privately bent, two legs protesting, person to person, her face flushed with a song and their little sleep. I give you back your heart. I give you permission - for the fuse inside her, throbbing angrily in the dirt, for the bitch in her and the burying of her wound - for the burying of her small red wound alive - for the pale flickering flare under her ribs, for the drunken sailor who waits in her left pulse, for the mother's knee, for the stocking, for the garter belt, for the call - the curious call when you will burrow in arms and breasts and tug at the orange ribbon in her hair and answer the call, the curious call. She is so naked and singular She is the sum of yourself and your dream. Climb her like a monument, step after step. She is solid. As for me, I am a watercolor. I wash off.

One day, Mommy saw a wild ant. Mommy wanted to take a closer look, so she slowly closed her eyes. She heard a little scurry, and when she opened her eyes, the wild ant was gone! Mommy looked around for the wild ant for a few minutes, but there was no sign of it.

Mommy was so sad that she missed her chance to see the wild ant up close. But then something amazing happened. Another wild ant scurried across the floor! Mommy quickly closed her eyes again. When she opened them, she saw the wild ant running along the wall. She was so happy!

Mommy watched the wild ant for a few minutes as it ran and scurried around the room. It was so interesting. Then, the wild ant disappeared into a small crack in the wall. Mommy was sad to see the wild ant go, but so thankful she got to watch it up close.

Once there was a girl named Lily. She was three years old. She knew lots of people, but nobody ever seemed too friendly.

But one day, a nice stranger came to talk to her. He smiled and offered her a beautiful flower. He said, "Lily, I want to give you this flower."

Lily was confused. She had never seen such a beautiful flower before. She looked at the stranger, then back at the flower, then back at the stranger.

Finally, Lily said thank you and took the flower. She was so happy to have something so special!

The stranger smiled and said, "You are very welcome! I just wanted to offer you something special." Then he turned and walked away.

Lily was so happy, she ran inside and showed her mom the flower. It was a beautiful white lily, and Lily smiled and hugged it all day.

Once upon a time there was a girl who wanted to watch TV. But her mom didn't allow it. This made the girl very frustrated.

She started to cry.

"Mommy," she cried, "please let me watch!"

But her mom said no, explaining she was too young to watch television.

This made the girl even more frustrated. She started to stomp her feet and cry even harder.

Finally, her mom said, "Okay, you can watch a little bit, but then you have to do something else."

The girl was so happy! She ran to the TV and began to watch. Her mom smiled at her daughter's joy.

The girl watched her show, and when it was done she thanked her mom. Her mom gave her a hug and said, "You better get ready for bed now."

The girl hugged her mom back and went to get ready for bed. She was much less frustrated now that she was allowed to watch TV.

name_of_work: The Vast Hour by Genevieve Taggard
content: All essences of sweetness from the white Warm day go up in vapor, when the dark Comes down. Ascends the tune of meadow-lark, Ascends the noon-time smell of grass, when night Takes sunlight from the world, and gives it ease. Mysterious wings have brushed the air; and light Float all the ghosts of sense and sound and sight; The silent hive is echoing the bees. So stir my thoughts at this slow, solemn time. Now only is there certainty for me When all the day's distilled and understood. Now light meets darkness: now my tendrils climb In this vast hour, up the living tree, Where gloom foregathers, and the stern winds brood.

Once upon a time, there was a wise old man who lived in a small village. He provided lots of help to all the people who lived there. 

He would listen to their worries and solve their problems. He wasn't just great at giving advice, he was also very generous. He was always willing to provide food and warm clothing to those who needed it. 

The old man showed the villagers the value of kindness and love. He used positive words and acted wisely to everyone he met. His thoughtfulness made everyone in the village so happy and grateful. 

The old man gave everyone an important lesson about life; that it is much more rewarding to help others than to do something for yourself. He showed that the most valuable thing you can give someone is your kindness.

One day there was a yellow dog. His name was Rudy. Rudy was walking around the house looking for something to do. Suddenly he heard a loud noise. It scared him. He ran quickly to the table. It was bigger than him, so he felt safe underneath it.

The noise continued. Rudy was very scared. He wanted to know what it was. He called out for his owner, "Mommy, what is that noise?".

Mommy came over and put her hand on Rudy's head. She thought for a moment and then said, "It's just the washing machine, Rudy. It's nothing to be scared of. Can you hear it?"

Rudy listened carefully and heard the washing machine spinning and humming. He wasn't scared anymore. He felt so happy that he gave Mommy a big kiss and a big hug. 

The end.

Jamie was hungry. She had not eaten anything today. Jamie was looking for something to eat. Then she saw a port. It was big and looked yummy!

Jamie moved closer to inspect the port. She wanted to eat it. But the port was too high for her to reach. She was so sad, she started to cry.

Suddenly, an idea came to Jamie. She thought of a plan! She jumped up and down. Up and down. With every jump, she got a bit higher.

Gradually, Jamie was able to increase her height. After a few jumps, she was tall enough to reach the port. She grabbed it with a big smile and ate it all up.

After she finished, Jamie was feeling full and happy. She went off to play, no longer hungry.

Tom was a boy who liked to play with his toys. He had a big box of toys in his room. He had cars, trains, dolls, blocks, and books. He also had a feather that he found in the park. He liked to tickle his nose with the feather and make funny noises.

One day, Tom was playing with his feather in his room. He heard a knock on the door. He thought it was his mom or dad. He said, "Come in!" But it was not his mom or dad. It was a big, scary monster. The monster had sharp teeth, long claws, and red eyes. The monster saw Tom and his feather. The monster wanted the feather. The monster said, "Give me the feather, or I will eat you!"

Tom was very scared. He did not want to give the monster his feather. He liked his feather. He said, "No, this is my feather. Go away!" He tried to run to the door, but the monster was faster. The monster grabbed Tom and his feather. The monster said, "Too bad, this is my feather now. And you are my snack!" The monster opened his mouth and bit Tom. Tom screamed, but no one heard him. The monster ate Tom and his feather. The monster was happy. Tom was gone. The end.

Once upon a time there was a little boy named Ben. He wanted to make a cake for his friend's birthday, so he asked his mom for help. His mom told him that if he was careful and did not smash the ingredients he could make the cake. Ben was excited and agreed to be careful. 

He mixed the ingredients and placed the cake in the the oven to bake. Then, Ben waited and waited. Finally, after some time, it was time to take out the cake. 

When Ben opened the oven, he found the cake was flipped upside down. Ben was so disappointed and started to cry. He asked his mom, "Why did the cake flip over? I was careful and I minded what you said!" 

His mom hugged him and said, "I know you were careful and minded what I said, but Ben, sometimes things don't go as planned. What's important is that you tried your best and remain flexible. As long as you have a flexible attitude and try your best, even when things don't go as planned, you can still be proud of yourself." 

Ben smiled, thanked his mom and agreed to remain flexible.

The moral of the story is that even when things don't turn out the way you had hoped, being flexible and trying your best is whatâ€™s most important.

Ben and Lily were playing in the park. They liked to slide, swing and run. They saw a big pile of leaves. They wanted to jump in it.

"Let's go, Ben!" Lily said. "It looks fun!"

They ran to the pile of leaves and jumped in. They laughed and threw leaves in the air. They felt something hard under the leaves. They moved the leaves and saw a skeleton.

"Ah!" Ben screamed. "It's a scary skeleton!"

Lily was not scared. She looked at the skeleton. It was brown and had no eyes, nose or hair. It had a big smile.

"It's not scary, Ben," Lily said. "It's just a skeleton. It can't hurt us. Maybe it was a nice person before."

Ben was still scared. He wanted to run away. He did not like the skeleton.

"No, Lily, it's scary!" Ben said. "Let's go away!"

Lily did not want to go. She wanted to hug the skeleton. She thought it was lonely and needed a friend.

"Please, Ben, don't go," Lily said. "Let's hug the skeleton. Maybe it will be happy."

Ben did not want to hug the skeleton. He thought it was cold and creepy. He did not want to make it happy.

"No, Lily, don't hug it!" Ben said. "It might bite you!"

Lily did not listen to Ben. She hugged the skeleton. It did not bite her. It did not move. It just smiled.

"See, Ben, it's not scary," Lily said. "It's nice. You can hug it too."

Ben looked at Lily and the skeleton. He saw that Lily was happy. He saw that the skeleton was not scary. He felt sorry for the skeleton. He decided to hug it too.

He hugged the skeleton. It did not bite him. It did not move. It just smiled.

"See, Lily, you were right," Ben said. "It's nice. I'm sorry I was scared."

Lily and Ben hugged the skeleton. They felt happy. They made a new friend. They played with the skeleton and the leaves. They had fun.

Once upon a time, a little girl named Sally was playing in her backyard. She saw a fierce figure passing by. She wondered what it was and asked her mom, "Mommy, what was that figure?"

Her mom replied, "That was a wolf, Sally. He's very fierce and he lives in the forest."

Sally thought of a plan and said, "I can go pass him and show him I'm brave!"

Her mom shook her head and said, "No, that would be very dangerous! Wolves can be very fierce and you would not be safe if you passed him."

Sally was sad, but her mom gave her a hug and said, "We'll find some other way to show off your bravery."

So, Sally and her mom thought of a plan and they decided to go on a hike and explore the forest. Sally was very brave, and she was able to explore the forest without getting hurt. She learned all about the fierce figures passing by and she was proud of herself for being so brave.

Once upon a time, there was an old lady. She had a plan to eat lunch with her friend. But then, something unexpected happened. Her friend had to delay their lunch for a little bit.

The old lady was very sad. She waited and waited for her friend. She just wanted to start eating lunch. Finally, the old lady saw her friend coming. They were so happy to see each other.

The old lady and her friend had a lot of fun at lunch. They talked, laughed, and ate lots of delicious food. It was the best lunch they ever had!

The old lady was glad that she didn't have to delay lunch anymore. They had a wonderful time together!

Jill and Tom were twins who liked to play in the garden. One day, they saw a big purple pot on the porch. They wondered what was inside.

"Let's look!" Jill said.

"No, it's Mom's pot. She said not to touch it." Tom said.

But Jill did not listen. She ran to the pot and gazed inside. She saw something shiny and round. She reached out to grab it.

"Jill, stop!" Tom shouted.

But it was too late. The shiny thing was a ball of fire. It burned Jill's hand and made a loud noise. The pot broke into pieces. Mom came out and saw the mess.

"Jill, Tom, what have you done?" Mom said. She was very angry and sad. She took Jill to the doctor and Tom to his room. She said they were in big trouble.

Jill and Tom felt sorry and scared. They wished they had listened to Mom and left the pot alone. They learned a hard lesson. The end.

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Polly. Polly was three years old and she loved to go outside and explore the big world around her. One day while she was out walking, she came to a street.

Polly carefully balanced her way down the street, welcoming each new challenge as she stepped from one foot to the other. Suddenly, a loud car startled her, and she stumbled.

"Oh no!" shouted Polly, as she fell onto the street. A kind man walked over to help her. 

"Are you alright?" he asked in a gentle, patient voice.

"Yes," said Polly. She was a bit scared, but the man's kind demeanor made her feel better.

The man offered to help Polly get back on her feet and Polly said yes. She held on to him as he balanced her back to safety. 

Unfortunately, the man was not as kind as he seemed. As soon as they reached the other side of the street, he grabbed Polly and ran away. 

Polly cried and screamed but no one was around to save her. She was never seen again.

One day, a cat and a dog were playing. They liked to run and play all day. The cat was fast, and the dog was strong.

The cat said, "Let's play a game. I will try to catch you, and you will try to catch me. If I catch you, you will go to jail." The dog agreed, and they started to play.

The dog ran after the cat, but the cat was too fast. The cat caught the dog and took him to jail. The jail was cold, and the dog did not like it.

The dog said, "Please let me out. I promise to play nice." The cat thought about it and decided to let the dog out of the cold jail.

They played together and had fun. They learned to be kind and play nice with each other.

Once upon a time, there was a little bird named Tweetie. Tweetie loved to sing songs all day long. One day, Tweetie saw a big gray cloud in the sky. "Oh no!" Tweetie said, "I think it might rain soon." 

Just then, Tweetie heard a whisper. "Don't worry, little bird," said a friendly voice. It was a wise old owl named Hootie. "I know a secret way to keep you dry in the rain." 

"What is it?" asked Tweetie. 

Hootie leaned in close and whispered the secret to Tweetie. "Sing a happy song and the rain will stay away," he said. 

Tweetie smiled and began to sing a joyful song. The rain never came and Tweetie was happy and dry. From that day on, Tweetie sang every day and never forgot Hootie's secret.

name_of_work: A November Night by Sara Teasdale
content: There! See the line of lights, A chain of stars down either side the street -- Why can't you lift the chain and give it to me, A necklace for my throat? I'd twist it round And you could play with it. You smile at me As though I were a little dreamy child Behind whose eyes the fairies live. . . . And see, The people on the street look up at us All envious. We are a king and queen, Our royal carriage is a motor bus, We watch our subjects with a haughty joy. . . . How still you are! Have you been hard at work And are you tired to-night? It is so long Since I have seen you -- four whole days, I think. My heart is crowded full of foolish thoughts Like early flowers in an April meadow, And I must give them to you, all of them, Before they fade. The people I have met, The play I saw, the trivial, shifting things That loom too big or shrink too little, shadows That hurry, gesturing along a wall, Haunting or gay -- and yet they all grow real And take their proper size here in my heart When you have seen them. . . . There's the Plaza now, A lake of light! To-night it almost seems That all the lights are gathered in your eyes, Drawn somehow toward you. See the open park Lying below us with a million lamps Scattered in wise disorder like the stars. We look down on them as God must look down On constellations floating under Him Tangled in clouds. . . . Come, then, and let us walk Since we have reached the park. It is our garden, All black and blossomless this winter night, But we bring April with us, you and I; We set the whole world on the trail of spring. I think that every path we ever took Has marked our footprints in mysterious fire, Delicate gold that only fairies see. When they wake up at dawn in hollow tree-trunks And come out on the drowsy park, they look Along the empty paths and say, "Oh, here They went, and here, and here, and here! Come, see, Here is their bench, take hands and let us dance About it in a windy ring and make A circle round it only they can cross When they come back again!" . . . Look at the lake -- Do you remember how we watched the swans That night in late October while they slept? Swans must have stately dreams, I think. But now The lake bears only thin reflected lights That shake a little. How I long to take One from the cold black water -- new-made gold To give you in your hand! And see, and see, There is a star, deep in the lake, a star! Oh, dimmer than a pearl -- if you stoop down Your hand could almost reach it up to me. . . . There was a new frail yellow moon to-night -- I wish you could have had it for a cup With stars like dew to fill it to the brim. . . . How cold it is! Even the lights are cold; They have put shawls of fog around them, see! What if the air should grow so dimly white That we would lose our way along the paths Made new by walls of moving mist receding The more we follow. . . . What a silver night! That was our bench the time you said to me The long new poem -- but how different now, How eerie with the curtain of the fog Making it strange to all the friendly trees! There is no wind, and yet great curving scrolls Carve themselves, ever changing, in the mist. Walk on a little, let me stand here watching To see you, too, grown strange to me and far. . . . I used to wonder how the park would be If one night we could have it all alone -- No lovers with close arm-encircled waists To whisper and break in upon our dreams. And now we have it! Every wish comes true! We are alone now in a fleecy world; Even the stars have gone. We two alone!

Once upon a time, there was a little birdie named Tweet. Tweet liked to fly around and sing a lot. One day, Tweet saw a big tree with a lot of ash on it. Tweet didn't know what ash was, but it looked like snow to her. She flew down to take a closer look.

Suddenly, Tweet felt very tired and wanted to take a nap. She decided to take a nap on the tree with the ash. But when she woke up, she couldn't breathe. The ash had covered her and she couldn't fly away. She was very scared and tried to call for help, but it was too quiet. 

Poor Tweet was trapped and couldn't escape. She wished she had never taken a nap on that tree. The end.

Once upon a time there was a cool fox called Joe. Joe was very dependable and was always looking to help. Every day he went out and looked for something delicious to eat. 

One day while Joe was out, he saw a big piece of meat. It was sitting in the middle of the road and Joe was very hungry. So he decided to take the meat home. When he got back to his den, he shared the meat with all of his friends. 

Joe's friends were very happy, but one of them said, "Joe, why didnâ€™t you keep this meat for yourself? You need to be a little selfish sometimes". But Joe replied, "It's important to think about others and help them out. If we all help each other, we will all be happier". 

Joe was right. By helping his friends, he made them feel special and important. Helping others is always a good thing and can bring a lot of joy to all. Joe showed us that being dependable and looking to help those in need are important values to have.

Sara liked to draw with her crayons. She made many images of her family, her friends, and her toys. She was very proud of her images and showed them to everyone. She thought they were very pretty.

One day, she went to play with Lily, her neighbor. Lily also liked to draw, but she used markers instead of crayons. She had many colors and made images of flowers, animals, and stars. She thought they were very pretty too.

Sara and Lily decided to share their images and see what they had drawn. Sara showed Lily her image of her mom and dad. Lily said, "That's nice, but your mom's hair is too yellow and your dad's nose is too big. My mom and dad are more pretty. Look at my image of them."

Lily showed Sara her image of her mom and dad. Sara said, "That's nice, but your mom's eyes are too green and your dad's mouth is too small. My mom and dad are more pretty. Look at my image of them again."

Sara and Lily started to argue about whose images were more pretty. They did not like each other's images and did not want to play anymore. They said, "You are not my friend. Go away."

Sara and Lily were very sad and angry. They did not have fun. They did not welcome each other.

Then, Sara's mom came to pick her up. She saw Sara and Lily crying and asked what happened. Sara and Lily told her about their images and their fight. Sara's mom said, "I'm sorry you had a fight, but you know, everyone can draw in different ways. There is no right or wrong way to make images. You can both make pretty images with your own colors and shapes. You don't have to like the same things, but you can still be friends and welcome each other."

Sara and Lily thought about what Sara's mom said. They realized that she was right. They looked at their images again and saw that they were both pretty in their own ways. They said, "You are right, mom. We are sorry we fought. We can both make pretty images and be friends. Can we play again?"

Sara's mom smiled and said, "Of course you can. I'm glad you made up. You are both very good at drawing. Why don't you make a new image together and welcome each other with a hug?"

Sara and Lily nodded and hugged each other. They said, "We are sorry. We are friends. We welcome each other."

They took their crayons and markers and made a new image together. They drew a big heart with their names inside. They showed it to Sara's mom and said, "Look, mom. This is our image of friendship. It is very pretty."

Sara's mom said, "Yes, it is very pretty. And so are you. I'm proud of you."

name_of_work: The Day is Done by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
content: The day is done, and the darkness Falls from the wings of Night, As a feather is wafted downward From an eagle in his flight. I see the lights of the village Gleam through the rain and the mist, And a feeling of sadness comes o'er me That my soul cannot resist: A feeling of sadness and longing, That is not akin to pain, And resembles sorrow only As the mist resembles the rain. Come, read to me some poem, Some simple and heartfelt lay, That shall soothe this restless feeling, And banish the thoughts of day. Not from the grand old masters, Not from the bards sublime, Whose distant footsteps echo Through the corridors of Time. For, like strains of martial music, Their mighty thoughts suggest Life's endless toil and endeavor; And to-night I long for rest. Read from some humbler poet, Whose songs gushed from his heart, As showers from the clouds of summer, Or tears from the eyelids start; Who, through long days of labor, And nights devoid of ease, Still heard in his soul the music Of wonderful melodies. Such songs have power to quiet The restless pulse of care, And come like the benediction That follows after prayer. Then read from the treasured volume The poem of thy choice, And lend to the rhyme of the poet The beauty of thy voice. And the night shall be filled with music, And the cares, that infest the day, Shall fold their tents, like the Arabs, And as silently steal away.

content: A Stranger came to the door at eve, And he spoke the bridegroom fair. He bore a green-white stick in his hand, And, for all burden, care. One day he showed the book to his mom. His mom became very angry. She took the book away and told the boy not to ever look at it again.

After a few minutes he felt better. He realized his mom was just looking out for him. He understood why she was angry. He knew it wasn't ok to look at the book.

So the boy never looked at the book again. He was happy to listen to his mom.

Sandy was a curious three year old girl. One day, she was playing with her toy car when her mom came out of the house with a box. When Sandy opened the box, she found a very special model inside. 

She had never seen anything like it before. It was bright and colourful, and it had small wings that twinkled when she moved them. Sandy wanted to try it out right away, but her mom said she needed to be careful. 

Sandy went into the garden and started to play with her new model. She picked it up and flew it around, but it kept slipping out of her hands. Eventually, Sandy gave up and tried to resist the urge to keep playing. 

Suddenly, something amazing happened. The model flew around Sandy in perfect circles and then flew back into her hands. Sandy was so surprised, she jumped up and down with joy. 

Sandy had found a way to make the model fly. She was a curious and determined girl, and she had managed to make the model do what she wanted it to. The model belonged to Sandy forever.

Once upon a time there was a boy. He was very happy. He went to the store and saw lots of tasty things. He wanted to buy them all so he could have a healthy snack. He had some money, but it wasn't enough for all the snacks he wanted.

The boy started to cry. He wanted to get all the snacks so badly. Then, an idea came to him. He grabbed all of his money and threw it in the air. He watched as the coins flew up high and then rained back down everywhere. 

The boy clapped his hands excitedly. He ran around the store and scooped up as many healthy snacks as he could. He was so happy. Now he had enough snacks to eat every day. He thanked the store and was on his way. 

The boy looked back one more time before he left. He knew he had made the right decision. He smiled and waved goodbye to the store. He was happy with his healthy snacks!

Once upon a time, there was a baby called Winnie. She was three years old and loved to explore the world around her.

One day she was in the park with her Mom and they both saw a small shop. Winnie was curious and asked her Mom if she could go inside. Mom agreed and so Winnie opened the door and stepped in.

Inside, Winnie found lots of things to look at, including something special - a very big and heavy menu. She picked it up and opened it to see what was inside. On the menu were all sorts of delicious looking food!

"Wow!" said Winnie, amazed by all the yummy things. 

"Can I have a hamburger please mom?" She asked.

"Yes", said Mom, "Let's go and order one now."

Winnie was so happy, she couldn't wait to eat the yummy hamburger!

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Sue. She was three years old and lived in a tidy house with her mom and dad. One morning, Sue was getting ready to take a bath. She hopped in the bathtub and started to play.

Suddenly, Sue had an idea. She asked her mom, "Can I record me in the bathtub?" Her mom smiled and said yes.

Sue was so excited. She splashed around in the tub and talked about all of her favorite things. She made funny noises, sang songs and recited rhymes. She even made bubbles that flew all around.

When Sue was done recording, she dried off and got dressed. She showed the recording to her mom. Her mom was happy to see how neat and tidy Sue had kept the bathroom while she was recording. She smiled and said, "Now that's a great recording!"

Sue was so proud of herself. From that day on, she would record all sorts of things in her neat and tidy house.

Tim and Mia liked to play in the park. They liked to swing, slide and run. One day, they saw a big rope hanging from a tree. It looked like fun.

"Let's swing on the rope!" Tim said.

"OK!" Mia said.

They ran to the rope and took turns to swing. They felt like they were flying in the air.

But the rope was old and weak. It had a small tear that Tim and Mia did not see. It was about to break.

A man was walking his dog in the park. He saw the children swinging on the rope. He knew it was dangerous.

"Hey, kids, be careful!" he shouted. "That rope is not safe. It might snap!"

He tried to warn them, but they did not hear him. They were having too much fun.

The man ran to them as fast as he could. He hoped he would reach them in time.

But he was too late.

The rope broke with a loud snap. Tim and Mia fell to the ground with a thud.

They cried out in pain and fear. They had bruises and scratches all over.

The man and his dog reached them and helped them up. He checked if they were OK.

"I'm sorry, kids, I tried to warn you," he said. "That rope was old and weak. You should not swing on it."

Tim and Mia nodded. They were sorry, too. They learned their lesson.

They thanked the man and his dog for helping them. They hugged each other and limped back to their parents.

They never swung on a rope again.

Lyric night of the lingering Indian Summer, Shadowy fields that are scentless but full of singing, Never a bird, but the passionless chant of insects, Ceaseless, insistent. The grasshopper's horn, and far-off, high in the maples, The wheel of a locust leisurely grinding the silence Under a moon waning and worn, broken, Tired with summer. Let me remember you, voices of little insects, Weeds in the moonlight, fields that are tangled with asters, Let me remember, soon will the winter be on us, Snow-hushed and heavy. Over my soul murmur your mute benediction, While I gaze, O fields that rest after harvest, As those who part look long in the eyes they lean to, Lest they forget them.

Lily was playing with her doll in her room. She liked to pretend that her doll was a princess and she was her friend. She had a small box that she used as a treasure chest. She put a shiny key inside the box and locked it. She said to her doll, "This is our secret. No one can open the box without the key."

But then she heard a loud sneeze from the hallway. It was her brother, Max. He had a cold and he was looking for a tissue. He saw Lily's door open and he walked in. He saw the box on the floor and he was curious. He picked it up and shook it. He heard something rattle inside. He said, "What is this? What is in here?"

Lily saw Max with her box and she was angry. She ran to him and tried to grab the box. She said, "No, Max, that is mine! That is my treasure! Give it back!" But Max was bigger and stronger. He held the box high above his head. He said, "No, Lily, this is mine now. I want to see what is in here. Maybe it is something cool."

Lily started to cry. She said, "Please, Max, please. That is my key. That is my special key. I need it for my doll. She is a princess and she needs her key." But Max did not listen. He tried to open the box with his fingers. But the lock was too tight. He said, "This is a stupid box. It does not open. I need something to break it."

He looked around the room and he saw a pair of scissors on the desk. He said, "Aha, I found it. I will use this to open the box." He ran to the desk and grabbed the scissors. He was about to cut the box when he heard a voice behind him. It was Mom. She said, "Max, what are you doing? Put down those scissors. They are not available for you. They are dangerous. And why are you holding Lily's box? Did you ask her if you can play with it?"

Max turned around and saw Mom. He felt scared and guilty. He said, "I'm sorry, Mom. I just wanted to see what was in the box. Lily said it was her treasure and she had a key. I wanted to see the key." Mom said, "Well, you should have asked her nicely. You should not take things that are not yours. And you should not use scissors to open things. You could hurt yourself or the box. Now, give the box back to Lily and say you are sorry."

Max gave the box back to Lily and said he was sorry. Lily hugged the box and said thank you. She opened the box with her key and showed Max the key. She said, "This is my key. It is shiny and pretty. It is for my doll. She is a princess and she needs her key." Max said, "Wow, that is a nice key. Can I see it?" Lily said, "Yes, you can see it. But you have to be gentle and careful. And you have to ask me first." Max said, "OK, I will. Thank you, Lily. You are a good sister." Lily said, "You are welcome, Max. You are a good brother. But you need a tissue. You still have a cold. Come on, let's go find one." They both smiled and walked out of the room. Mom followed them and said, "That's better. I'm proud of you both. Now, let's get some juice and cookies. They are available in the kitchen." They all went to the kitchen and had a snack. They were happy and they forgot about the sneeze.

name_of_work: Photograph of Haymaker, 1890 by Molly Holden
content: It is not so much the image of the man that's moving -- he pausing from his work to whet his scythe, trousers tied below the knee, white shirt lit by another summer's sun, another century's -- as the sight of the grasses beyond his last laid swathe, so living yet upon the moment previous to death; for as the man stooping straightened up and bent again they died before his blade. Sweet hay and gone some seventy years ago and yet they stand before me in the sun, stems damp still where their neighbours' fall uncovered them, succulent and straight, immediate with moon-daisies

Once there was an ugly pillow. He was all by himself, so he was very sad. Every day he said to himself, "I wish someone would come and wash me." 
Then one day, a little girl named Daisy heard him say this, and she stopped and said, "I will wash you!" She brought him to the sink and started rubbing him with soapy bubbles. She was very gentle and it felt so nice. 

When she finished washing the pillow, he looked so much cleaner, brighter, shinier. He felt so happy! Daisy brought him back to his spot and hugged him tight. 
 
From that day forward, Daisy always made sure to wash the pillow twice a week. She liked having a clean and happy pillow around. He never felt so lucky!

Tommy was playing with his toy cars in his room. He liked to make them zoom and crash on the floor. He did not hear his mom call him for bath time. She came to his room and saw the mess.

"Tommy, it's time for your bath. Put away your cars and come with me," she said.

"But I don't want a bath. I want to play more," Tommy said. He held his cars tight and did not move.

Mom was not happy. She took his cars and put them on the shelf. She urged Tommy to get up and follow her. She said, "You need a bath to be clean and fresh. You can play with your cars again tomorrow. Now, let's go."

Tommy was sad and angry. He did not like to leave his cars. He did not like to be wet and soapy. He walked slowly behind his mom. He hoped she would change her mind.

But she did not. She filled the bathtub with warm water and bubbles. She put Tommy in the water and gave him a washcloth and a rubber duck. She said, "Look, you have a duck to play with. And the bubbles are fun. You can make shapes and pop them. Try it."

Tommy looked at the duck and the bubbles. He did not want to admit it, but they looked a little fun. He took the duck and squeezed it. It made a quack sound. He smiled. He dipped the washcloth in the water and made it wet. He threw it in the air and watched it fall. He laughed.

Mom smiled too. She said, "See, bath time is not so bad. You can have fun and be clean at the same time. Now, let me wash your hair and then you can play some more."

Tommy nodded. He let mom wash his hair and rinse it. He did not cry or fuss. He felt the water and the bubbles on his skin. He felt good. He said, "Thank you, mom. I like bath time."

Mom hugged him and said, "You're welcome, Tommy. I'm proud of you. You're a good boy. Now, let's get you dry and put on your pajamas. Then we can read a story before bed."

Tommy agreed. He got out of the bathtub and wrapped himself in a towel. He felt warm and cozy. He followed mom to his room. He saw his cars on the shelf. He did not miss them so much. He was ready for bed. He said, "Mom, can you read me the story about the big red car?"

Mom said, "Of course, Tommy. I love that story. Let's go to your bed and I'll read it to you."

They went to his bed and mom opened the book. She read the story about the big red car and its adventures. Tommy listened and imagined. He felt happy and sleepy. He closed his eyes and drifted to sleep. Mom kissed him and said, "Good night, Tommy. I love you."

Tommy murmured, "I love you too, mom. Good night."

Once upon a time, there was a wise old owl. He lived in a big tree in the forest. The owl loved to blink his big eyes and watch the little animals play.

One day, he saw a small bunny hopping near the tree. The bunny had a shiny buckle on his collar. The wise owl blinked and looked closer. He saw that the buckle was stuck on a branch.

The owl wanted to help the bunny. He blinked his eyes, flew down from the tree, and used his beak to free the buckle. The bunny was very happy and thanked the wise owl.

From that day on, the wise owl and the bunny became good friends. They played together in the forest, and the owl always blinked his eyes to watch over his little friend.

name_of_work: Fiddler Jones by Edgar Lee Masters
content: The earth keeps some vibration going There in your heart, and that is you. And if the people find you can fiddle, Why, fiddle you must, for all your life. What do you see, a harvest of clover? Or a meadow to walk through to the river? The wind's in the corn; you rub your hands For beeves hereafter ready for market; Or else you hear the rustle of skirts Like the girls when dancing at Little Grove. To Cooney Potter a pillar of dust Or whirling leaves meant ruinous drouth; They looked to me like Red-Head Sammy Stepping it off, to "Toor-a-Loor." How could I till my forty acres Not to speak of getting more, With a medley of horns, bassoons and piccolos Stirred in my brain by crows and robins And the creak of a wind-mill--only these? And I never started to plow in my life That some one did not stop in the road And take me away to a dance or picnic. I ended up with forty acres; I ended up with a broken fiddle-- And a broken laugh, and a thousand memories, And not a single regret.

name_of_work: Epic Simile by A. E. Stallings
content: Right shoulder aching with day-long butchery, Left shoulder numb with dints clanged on the shield, The hero is fouled with blood, his own and others', First slick, then sticky, then caked, starting to mat His beard--the armor deadweight all around him; His teeth grit and rattle with every jolt Of bronze-rimmed wheels behind the shit-flecked horses. But when he glimpses the mountains, the distant snow, A blankness swoons upon him, and he hears Nothing but the white vowels of the wind Brushing through stands of spears like conifers While a banner slips its staff and hangs in the blue Like a kestrel or a contrail. The hero's death, The prize, elusive quarry of his life, Stands stock-still in her cloven tracks in snow And turns, one ear tuned to the creek's far bank, One dished towards him. Her unstartled gaze Beads on him like a sniper's sights, until At the clean report of a cracking poplar branch, She leaps away like luck, over rapid water, And snowfall scrims the scene like a mist of tears, Like a migraine, like sweat or blood streaming into your eyes.

Tom and Mary were best friends. One day, Tom was frustrated because his toy was broken and he didn't know how to save it. Mary grabbed an orange from her bag and said to Tom, "Let's try this!" Tom tried to use the orange to fix his toy, but nothing worked.

Tom got even more frustrated and started to cry. Mary tried to calm him down, but she didn't know what to do. She tried to think of another way to save Tom's toy, but nothing worked.

Suddenly, Tom came up with an idea. "How about using magic? It could save my toy!" he exclaimed. Mary was hesitant but eventually agreed.

They grabbed a wand from her bag and waved it around the toy. But unfortunately, the toy still did not work. Tom was so frustrated that he started to cry again.

Mary gave Tom a hug and said, "It's okay, Tom. I'm sorry, but we couldn't save your toy."

name_of_work: To have without holding by Marge Piercy
content: Learning to love differently is hard, love with the hands wide open, love with the doors banging on their hinges, the cupboard unlocked, the wind roaring and whimpering in the rooms rustling the sheets and snapping the blinds that thwack like rubber bands in an open palm. It hurts to love wide open stretching the muscles that feel as if they are made of wet plaster, then of blunt knives, then of sharp knives. It hurts to thwart the reflexes of grab, of clutch ; to love and let go again and again. It pesters to remember the lover who is not in the bed, to hold back what is owed to the work that gutters like a candle in a cave without air, to love consciously, conscientiously, concretely, constructively. I can't do it, you say it's killing me, but you thrive, you glow on the street like a neon raspberry, You float and sail, a helium balloon bright bachelor's button blue and bobbing on the cold and hot winds of our breath, as we make and unmake in passionate diastole and systole the rhythm of our unbound bonding, to have and not to hold, to love with minimized malice, hunger and anger moment by moment balanced.

name_of_work: O Were My Love Yon Lilac Fair by Robert Burns
content: O were my love yon Lilac fair, Wi' purple blossoms to the Spring, And I, a bird to shelter there, When wearied on my little wing! How I wad mourn when it was torn By Autumn wild, and Winter rude! But I wad sing on wanton wing, When youthfu' May its bloom renew'd. O gin my love were yon red rose, That grows upon the castle wa'; And I myself a drap o' dew, Into her bonie breast to fa'! O there, beyond expression blest, I'd feast on beauty a' the night; Seal'd on her silk-saft faulds to rest, Till fley'd awa by Phoebus' light!

Once upon a time, there was a grumpy bear who lived in the woods. He loved to spend time alone, away from all of the other animals in the forest.

One day, the bear was walking through the woods when he heard something snap. He looked up and saw a blue jacket hanging from a tree branch. He didn't know what it was, so he decided to take it.

The bear put on the jacket and went on his way. As he walked, he felt happy and warm. But soon, he began to feel grumpyâ€”the jacket was too tight! The bear tried to rip it off, but it wouldn't come off. He snapped and snapped, but it wouldn't come off!

Just then, a little rabbit came along and saw the bear in his tight jacket. The little rabbit said, "Oh no! Let me help you!" He used both of his paws and pulled, and the jacket came off in a snap!

The bear thanked the rabbit and went on his way, happy and free. He wouldn't forget the little rabbit who helped him with his grumpy jacket.

Anna and Ben like to play with their toys. They have a lot of toys, but their favorite is the big van. The van is red and shiny, and it has four wheels and a horn. Anna and Ben can make the van go fast or slow, and they can make it beep.

But sometimes, Anna is bossy. She wants to have the van all the time, and she does not let Ben play with it. She says, "I am the driver, and you are the passenger. You have to do what I say, or you can't play with the van." Ben does not like that. He wants to be the driver sometimes, too.

One day, Ben has an idea. He says to Anna, "Do you know what is in the back of the van?" Anna says, "No, what is it?" Ben says, "It is a surprise. You have to close your eyes and follow me." Anna is curious. She closes her eyes and holds Ben's hand. Ben leads her to the back of the van and opens the door.

But there is nothing in the back of the van. Ben quickly jumps in the front seat and closes the door. He says, "Ha ha, I tricked you. Now I am the driver, and you are the passenger. You have to do what I say, or you can't play with the van." Anna is angry. She says, "That is not fair. Give me the van back. You are mean." Ben says, "No, I am not mean. You are bossy. You have to share the van with me. We can take turns being the driver and the passenger. That is more fun."

Anna thinks for a moment. She knows that Ben is right. She says, "Okay, I am sorry. I will share the van with you. We can take turns being the driver and the passenger. That is more fun." Ben says, "Thank you. I am sorry, too. I will not trick you again. We can be friends." Anna and Ben smile and hug. They play with the van happily. They make it go fast and slow, and they make it beep. They have fun.

name_of_work: A Quoi Bon Dire by Charlotte Mew
content: Seventeen years ago you said Something that sounded like Good-bye; And everybody thinks that you are dead, But I. So I, as I grow stiff and cold To this and that say Good-bye too; And everybody sees that I am old But you. And one fine morning in a sunny lane Some boy and girl will meet and kiss and swear That nobody can love their way again While over there You will have smiled, I shall have tossed your hair.

Just as in the horror movies when someone discovers that the phone calls are coming from inside the house so too, I realized that our tender overlapping has been taking place only inside me. All that sweetness, the love and desire-- it's just been me dialing myself then following the ringing to another room to find no one on the line, well, sometimes a little breathing but more often than not, nothing. To think that all this time-- which would include the boat rides, the airport embraces, and all the drinks-- it's been only me and the two telephones, the one on the wall in the kitchen and the extension in the darkened guest room upstairs.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to draw and always carried her favorite pencil with her. One day, she met a boy named Max.

Max said, "I have a plan. Let's draw a picture of a fair together!"

Lily loved the idea and they started to draw. They drew a big ferris wheel, a carousel, and lots of people having fun. But suddenly, Lily accidentally broke her pencil.

"I can't finish the picture," she said sadly.

"Don't worry," said Max. "I have an extra pencil."

So they continued to draw, but when they finished, a gust of wind blew the picture away.

Lily and Max were very sad that their picture was gone. But they promised each other that they would plan another fair and draw it again.

Once upon a time, there was a shy animal. This animal was very scared of people and would always hide whenever someone came near. One day, the animal saw a big puddle of water and decided to take a drink. As it was drinking, a little girl came by and said hello. The animal was scared at first, but the girl was very nice and didn't try to hurt the animal. Instead, she splashed in the puddle with the animal and they had a lot of fun together. From that day on, the animal wasn't so shy anymore and would come out to play with the little girl whenever she came by.

One day, a small dog named Ben went to play in the park. Ben loved to run and jump in the grass. He had a lot of fun with his friends. They played ball, and they played tag. It was a sunny and happy day.

As they played, a big cat came to the park. The cat was rude. He walked up to Ben and his friends and said, "I want to play too!" But he did not ask nicely. Ben and his friends did not like the rude cat, but they let him play so he would not be sad.

While they played, the rude cat tried to snap at Ben's paw. Ben was scared and said, "No, don't do that! That hurts!" The cat stopped and said sorry. Ben and the cat became friends, and they all played together. The cat learned not to be rude, and they had a great day at the park.

Tommy liked to hop. He hopped in the morning, he hopped at noon, he hopped in the evening. He hopped with his friends, he hopped with his toys, he hopped with his dog. He hopped everywhere he could.

One day, he found a hat. It was a big hat, with a red feather. It was not an ordinary hat. It was a magic hat. Tommy put it on his head and hopped. He felt something strange. He looked around and saw that he was not in his yard anymore. He was in a forest, with tall trees and colorful birds.

"Wow!" he said. "This hat can take me to different places. I wonder where else I can go."

He hopped again and again, and each time he saw a new place. He saw a farm, with cows and pigs and chickens. He saw a beach, with sand and waves and shells. He saw a city, with cars and buses and buildings. He saw a lot of things he had never seen before.

He was having fun, but he also missed his home. He wanted to see his mom and dad and his dog. He wanted to play with his friends and his toys. He wanted to eat his favorite food and sleep in his own bed. He decided to hop one last time and go back to his yard.

He hopped and hopped, but nothing happened. He was still in the city, with the noise and the crowd. He tried to hop again, but the hat fell off his head. A man picked it up and ran away.

"Hey!" Tommy shouted. "That's my hat! Give it back!"

But the man did not hear him. He was gone. Tommy was sad and scared. He did not know how to get home without his hat. He did not know anyone in the city. He did not know what to do.

He sat on the sidewalk and cried. He wished he had never found the hat. He wished he had never hopped away from his home. He wished he had been happy with his ordinary life.
