Alice looked at the onion, frustrated. It was too hard to separate the layers of the onion. She knew that if she wanted to make the perfect soup, then she needed to separate them.

Her mum saw her struggling and asked, "Would you like help?"

Alice shook her head. She wanted to do it all by herself. She started to pull on the layers of the onion again.

Her mum watched her and said, "It often makes us cry when we separate onions."

Alice didn't understand what her mum meant by that. She kept trying and trying but she couldn't separate them.

Suddenly, her eyes started to fill with tears. She was surprised! She looked back at her mum, surprised and she said, "Mum, why am I crying?"

Her mum smiled and said, "It happens to all of us. The oils in the onions make us cry when we try and separate them - but you can do it!"

Alice wiped her tears away and tried again with renewed determination. She managed to separate the layers of the onion and was proud of herself. She smiled and shouted, "I did it!"

Once upon a time, there was a mommy and a daddy. They both wanted to raise something special. So they went to the store and got a sausage.

The mommy and daddy were so proud of their sausage. They cooked it together and made it all yummy. Everyone in the family said it was the best sausage they ever had.

Then something magical happened. After the mommy and daddy fed the sausage to the family, something began to grow in the garden. It was huge!

The mommy and daddy were very proud when they saw what the sausage had done. It had grown into a big vegetable garden! The mommy and daddy could now feed their whole family fresh vegetables. They were so glad they had raised the sausage.

WHAT is this life if, full of care, We have no time to stand and stare?-- No time to stand beneath the boughs, And stare as long as sheep and cows: No time to see, when woods we pass, Where squirrels hide their nuts in grass: No time to see, in broad daylight, Streams full of stars, like skies at night: No time to turn at Beauty's glance, And watch her feet, how they can dance: No time to wait till her mouth can Enrich that smile her eyes began? A poor life this if, full of care, We have no time to stand and stare.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. Lily had a pet mouse named Lucky. Lucky was very small and had soft, brown fur. 

One day, Lily was playing in her room when she saw Lucky run across the floor. She chased after him, but Lucky was too fast and ran under her bed. 

Lily got down on her hands and knees and looked under the bed. She saw Lucky hiding in a corner. Lucky was lucky because Lily loved him very much and took good care of him. 

Lily reached under the bed and gently picked up Lucky. She held him in her hands and gave him a little kiss on his head. Lucky was happy to be with Lily, his best friend in the whole world.

Once upon a time, there was a little puppy. The puppy was brown, like his nose and his eyes. He loved adventure.

One day, the puppy spotted something that looked fun up ahead. It was a deep brown hole! The little pup was excited. He knew he had to explore it. He went to the edge of the hole and took a deep breath. Then, he dived in! 

At first he was scared, but he soon began to have fun. He paddled around looking for something special. Suddenly, he found something sparkly in the water. He felt around with his paws and realized it was pepper! He picked it up, and quickly swam back to the surface.

When he reached the edge of the hole, he took a big, deep breath. Then, he jumped out with his prize in his mouth. He was so proud of himself for finding the pepper and for taking a big dive. He wagged his tail and ran off to show his family his new discovery.

name_of_work: Some One by Walter de la Mare
content: Some one came knocking At my wee, small door; Someone came knocking; I'm sure-sure-sure; I listened, I opened, I looked to left and right, But nought there was a stirring In the still dark night; Only the busy beetle Tap-tapping in the wall, Only from the forest The screech-owl's call, Only the cricket whistling While the dewdrops fall, So I know not who came knocking, At all, at all, at all.

Once upon a time there was a little girl. Her name was Lucy. She was only three years old and she loved to explore the world around her.

One day Lucy wanted to explore the ocean. She found a boat and asked her Dad if she could take it out. He said yes and off she went!

As soon as Lucy was out in the ocean, she saw a large and beautiful reef. She wanted to explore it, so she got closer to the reef.

Suddenly, Lucy noticed something frightening. It was a large fish! She was scared and scared to go any closer. She turned her boat around and bumped back home.

Lucy had a great adventure at the ocean, but she learned that there can be some frightening things out there! She will always remember to include being careful in her adventures.

Once upon a time, there was a little penguin named Pip. Pip lived in an igloo with his family. The igloo was tight, but it kept them warm.

One day, Pip found a shiny rock outside. He wanted to make it even shinier, so he decided to polish it. He rubbed and rubbed the rock until it was very shiny.

But when Pip went back inside the igloo, he accidentally knocked over a candle. The igloo caught on fire and Pip's family couldn't escape. Pip was very sad that he had caused the fire and lost his family.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She went on a trip with her family and had to pack her luggage. She put her clothes, toys, and snacks in her bag. Her mom said they needed to bring extra snacks to supply everyone on the trip. 

When they arrived at their destination, they went to a unique store. Lily saw a unique toy that she wanted, but her mom said they didn't have enough money to buy it. Lily was sad, but her mom said they could go on a treasure hunt to find unique things in nature instead. 

They went on a hike and found unique rocks, flowers, and animals. Lily was happy she found unique things without buying them. When they got back to their hotel, Lily's dad realized they forgot to bring toothpaste. Luckily, the hotel had a supply of toothpaste for them to use. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play pretend with her dolls and teddy bears. One day, she pretended to be a princess who lived in a big castle.

For dinner, the princess had broccoli. She didn't like it at first, but then she pretended that the broccoli was a magical tree that gave her powers. She ate it all up and felt strong and brave.

After dinner, the princess went to her delicate bed made of soft pillows and blankets. She cuddled with her teddy bear and fell asleep, dreaming of more magical adventures. The end.

name_of_work: A Certain Lady by Dorothy Parker
content: Oh, I can smile for you, and tilt my head, And drink your rushing words with eager lips, And paint my mouth for you a fragrant red, And trace your brows with tutored finger-tips. When you rehearse your list of loves to me, Oh, I can laugh and marvel, rapturous-eyed. And you laugh back, nor can you ever see, The thousand little deaths my heart has died. And you believe, so well I know my part, That I am gay as morning, light as snow, And all the straining things within my heart You'll never know. Oh, I can laugh and listen, when we meet, And you bring tales of fresh adventurings,-- Of ladies delicately indiscreet, Of lingering hands, and gently whispered things. And you are pleased with me, and strive anew To sing me sagas of your late delights. Thus do you want me--marveling, gay, and true, Nor do you see my staring eyes of nights. And when, in search of novelty, you stray, Oh, I can kiss you blithely as you go.... And what goes on, my love, while you're away, You'll never know.

Once upon a time, there was a fat bear. He lived in a forest with a lot of trees and animals. One day the bear was feeling very hungry. He looked around for something to eat and saw a long rope. He grabbed it with his big claws and took a big bite. The rope tasted bad and the bear's mouth started to hurt. He quickly let go and knew that he should have stayed away from it. 

The bear decided to look for something else to eat. He found a fat apple tree just a few steps away and started to eat the apples. He ate and ate until he was full. The bear was happy and content. He decided to take a rope for himself the next time he went on an adventure. 

The end.

name_of_work: Part VII: The Rime of The Ancient Mariner by S.T. Coleridge
content: This Hermit good lives in that wood Which slopes down to the sea. How loudly his sweet voice he rears! He loves to talk with marineres That come from a far countree. He kneels at morn, and noon, and eve-- He hath a cushion plump: It is the moss that wholly hides The rotted old oak-stump. The skiff-boat neared: I heard them talk, 'Why, this is strange, I trow! Where are those lights so many and fair, That signal made but now?' 'Strange, by my faith!' the Hermit said-- 'And they answered not our cheer! The planks looked warped! and see those sails, How thin they are and sere! I never saw aught like to them, Unless perchance it were Brown skeletons of leaves that lag My forest-brook along; When the ivy-tod is heavy with snow, And the owlet whoops to the wolf below, That eats the she-wolf's young.' 'Dear Lord! it hath a fiendish look-- (The Pilot made reply) I am a-feared'--'Push on, push on!' Said the Hermit cheerily. The boat came closer to the ship, But I nor spake nor stirred; The boat came close beneath the ship, And straight a sound was heard. Under the water it rumbled on, Still louder and more dread: It reached the ship, it split the bay; The ship went down like lead. Stunned by that loud and dreadful sound, Which sky and ocean smote, Like one that hath been seven days drowned My body lay afloat; But swift as dreams, myself I found Within the Pilot's boat. Upon the whirl, where sank the ship, The boat spun round and round; And all was still, save that the hill Was telling of the sound. I moved my lips--the Pilot shrieked And fell down in a fit; The holy Hermit raised his eyes, And prayed where he did sit. I took the oars: the Pilot's boy, Who now doth crazy go, Laughed loud and long, and all the while His eyes went to and fro. 'Ha! ha!' quoth he, 'full plain I see, The Devil knows how to row.' And now, all in my own countree, I stood on the firm land! The Hermit stepped forth from the boat, And scarcely he could stand. 'O shrieve me, shrieve me, holy man!' The Hermit crossed his brow. 'Say quick,' quoth he, 'I bid thee say-- What manner of man art thou?' Forthwith this frame of mine was wrenched With a woful agony, Which forced me to begin my tale; And then it left me free. Since then, at an uncertain hour, That agony returns: And till my ghastly tale is told, This heart within me burns. I pass, like night, from land to land; I have strange power of speech; That moment that his face I see, I know the man that must hear me: To him my tale I teach. What loud uproar bursts from that door! The wedding-guests are there: But in the garden-bower the bride And bride-maids singing are: And hark the little vesper bell, Which biddeth me to prayer! O Wedding-Guest! this soul hath been Alone on a wide wide sea: So lonely 'twas, that God himself Scarce seemed there to be. O sweeter than the marriage-feast, 'Tis sweeter far to me, To walk together to the kirk With a goodly company!-- To walk together to the kirk, And all together pray, While each to his great Father bends, Old men, and babes, and loving friends And youths and maidens gay! Farewell, farewell! but this I tell To thee, thou Wedding-Guest! He prayeth well, who loveth well Both man and bird and beast. He prayeth best, who loveth best All things both great and small; For the dear God who loveth us, He made and loveth all. The Mariner, whose eye is bright, Whose beard with age is hoar, Is gone: and now the Wedding-Guest Turned from the bridegroom's door. He went like one that hath been stunned, And is of sense forlorn: A sadder and a wiser man, He rose the morrow morn.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to swim and dive in the pool. One day, Timmy's mom said, "Timmy, it's time to go upstairs and get ready for bed." Timmy didn't want to leave the pool, but he knew he had to listen to his mom.

When they got upstairs, Timmy's mom helped him get into his comfortable pajamas. Timmy said, "Mommy, can I dive into my bed like I do in the pool?" His mom laughed and said, "No, Timmy, you might hurt yourself. But you can jump up and down on it if you want!"

Timmy had fun jumping on his bed until he got tired. Then his mom read him a story and he fell asleep. The next morning, Timmy couldn't wait to go back to the pool and dive again.

name_of_work: The Robber Bridegroom by Margaret Atwood
content: He would like not to kill. He would like what he imagines other men have, instead of this red compulsion. Why do the women fail him and die badly? He would like to kill them gently, finger by finger and with great tenderness, so that at the end they would melt into him with gratitude for his skill and the final pleasure he still believes he could bring them if only they would accept him, but they scream too much and make him angry. Then he goes for the soul, rummaging in their flesh for it, despotic with self-pity, hunting among the nerves and the shards of their faces for the one thing he needs to live, and lost back there in the poplar and spruce forest in the watery moonlight, where his young bride, pale but only a little frightened, her hands glimmering with his own approaching death, gropes her way towards him along the obscure path, from white stone to white stone, ignorant and singing, dreaming of him as he is.

Where sunless rivers weep Their waves into the deep, She sleeps a charmed sleep: Awake her not. Led by a single star, She came from very far To seek where shadows are Her pleasant lot. She left the rosy morn, She left the fields of corn, For twilight cold and lorn And water springs. Through sleep, as through a veil, She sees the sky look pale, And hears the nightingale That sadly sings. Rest, rest, a perfect rest Shed over brow and breast; Her face is toward the west, The purple land. She cannot see the grain Ripening on hill and plain; She cannot feel the rain Upon her hand. Rest, rest, for evermore Upon a mossy shore; Rest, rest at the heart's core Till time shall cease: Sleep that no pain shall wake; Night that no morn shall break Till joy shall overtake Her perfect peace.

Once there was a little bird who was feeling very lonely in the evening. He looked around and he could not find a single friend to play with. He felt so alone and sad, that he had to find something to do. All of a sudden he saw a star twinkling in the night sky! He was so very surprised, that his sadness had been replaced with a sense of joy.

He flew closer to the star and something unexpected happened. He saw he wasn't alone there! There were other birds that were playing together in the night sky. He felt so excited, that he did not hesistate to join them in a game of tag.

He spent the evening playing with his new friends and the loneliness had been replaced with joy. He was not alone anymore!

The little bird learned an important lesson that night. Even when you feel like you have no one to turn to, you should always look to the sky and remember there are always new friends near.

He stopped and looked at the clock. â€œThat looks like something I can useâ€, he thought. He quickly grabbed the clock and began to cover it in a blanket. 

Just then, he heard a voice from behind him. â€œWhat are you doing? That clock belongs to me!â€ It was his friend, the rabbit. 

The bear tried to cover up the rabbit's words. â€œNo, this clock is mine!â€ 

The rabbit shook her head. â€œNo, it's not. You're so selfish. I was looking for this clock and you just had to grab it!â€ 

The bear sighed. He realized his mistake and unwrapped the clock. He handed it to the rabbit. â€œSorry about that. Can I help you find something else to cover?â€ 

The rabbit smiled. â€œThat would be nice!â€ 

From then on, the bear always shared his things with his friends.

We are the music makers, And we are the dreamers of dreams, Wandering by lone sea-breakers, And sitting by desolate streams; -- World-losers and world-forsakers, On whom the pale moon gleams: Yet we are the movers and shakers Of the world for ever, it seems. With wonderful deathless ditties We build up the world's great cities, And out of a fabulous story We fashion an empire's glory: One man with a dream, at pleasure, Shall go forth and conquer a crown; And three with a new song's measure Can trample a kingdom down. We, in the ages lying, In the buried past of the earth, Built Nineveh with our sighing, And Babel itself in our mirth; And o'erthrew them with prophesying To the old of the new world's worth; For each age is a dream that is dying, Or one that is coming to birth. A breath of our inspiration Is the life of each generation; A wondrous thing of our dreaming Unearthly, impossible seeming -- The soldier, the king, and the peasant Are working together in one, Till our dream shall become their present, And their work in the world be done. They had no vision amazing Of the goodly house they are raising; They had no divine foreshowing Of the land to which they are going: But on one man's soul it hath broken, A light that doth not depart; And his look, or a word he hath spoken, Wrought flame in another man's heart. And therefore to-day is thrilling With a past day's late fulfilling; And the multitudes are enlisted In the faith that their fathers resisted, And, scorning the dream of to-morrow, Are bringing to pass, as they may, In the world, for its joy or its sorrow, The dream that was scorned yesterday. But we, with our dreaming and singing, Ceaseless and sorrowless we! The glory about us clinging Of the glorious futures we see, Our souls with high music ringing: O men! it must ever be That we dwell, in our dreaming and singing, A little apart from ye. For we are afar with the dawning And the suns that are not yet high, And out of the infinite morning Intrepid you hear us cry -- How, spite of your human scorning, Once more God's future draws nigh, And already goes forth the warning That ye of the past must die. Great hail! we cry to the comers From the dazzling unknown shore; Bring us hither your sun and your summers; And renew our world as of yore; You shall teach us your song's new numbers, And things that we dreamed not before: Yea, in spite of a dreamer who slumbers, And a singer who sings no more.

name_of_work: Dulce et Decorum Est by Wilfred Owen
content: Bent double, like old beggars under sacks, Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge, Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs, And towards our distant rest began to trudge. Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots, But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind; Drunk with fatigue; deaf even to the hoots Of gas-shells dropping softly behind. Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!--An ecstasy of fumbling Fitting the clumsy helmets just in time, But someone still was yelling out and stumbling And flound'ring like a man in fire or lime.-- Dim through the misty panes and thick green light, As under a green sea, I saw him drowning. In all my dreams before my helpless sight, He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning. If in some smothering dreams, you too could pace Behind the wagon that we flung him in, And watch the white eyes writhing in his face, His hanging face, like a devil's sick of sin; If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs, Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud Of vile, incurable sores on innocent tongues,-- My friend, you would not tell with such high zest To children ardent for some desperate glory, The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est Pro patria mori.

Caught in the center of a soundless field While hot inexplicable hours go by What trap is this? Where were its teeth concealed? You seem to ask. I make a sharp reply, Then clean my stick. I'm glad I can't explain Just in what jaws you were to suppurate: You may have thought things would come right again If you could only keep quite still and wait.

Once upon a time, there was a little green insect named Buzz. Buzz was always so excited to get the mail. Every day, Buzz would fly to the mailbox and eagerly await the mailman to bring the mail.

One day, when Buzz arrived at the mailbox, he was very surprised to find that there was something new - a big, shiny, red box. Buzz was so excited! He had never seen a box that looked so wonderful before.

Suddenly, a large gust of wind blew in and knocked the box over. Buzz quickly flew to the box and tried to put the pieces back together. Buzz was determined to make it work, but the box wouldn't fit back together no matter how hard he tried.

The wind started to pick up and Buzz was getting worried. He had to find a way to make the box stay together, or the mailman wouldn't be able to put the mail in it.

Just then, a kind voice said, "I can help you, Buzz". It was an older green insect flying down from a nearby tree. The older green insect used a few twigs and some leaves to tie the box together. With a yelp of joy, Buzz thanked the older green insect and watched as the mailman arrived and put all the mail into the box.

Buzz waved goodbye to the older green insect and watched the mailman fly off with a big smile on his face. This was the best

name_of_work: We Wear the Mask by Paul Laurence Dunbar
content: We wear the mask that grins and lies, It hides our cheeks and shades our eyes,-- This debt we pay to human guile; With torn and bleeding hearts we smile, And mouth with myriad subtleties. Why should the world be over-wise, In counting all our tears and sighs? Nay, let them only see us, while We wear the mask. We smile, but, O great Christ, our cries To thee from tortured souls arise. We sing, but oh the clay is vile Beneath our feet, and long the mile; But let the world dream otherwise, We wear the mask!

Mama and Daddy began to make plans for the rest of the day. Mama said to Daddy, â€œWe need to make sure that Kayla gets home in time for dinner. Can you remind her to get off the playground soon?â€

Daddy smiled and said, â€œSure, I can do that.â€ He then called out to Kayla, â€œHey, sweetie! What do you think about coming off the playground soon?â€

Kayla said, â€œNo, I donâ€™t want to. I like the structure here and Iâ€™m having so much fun!â€

Mama and Daddy looked at each other in surprise. They never expected Kayla to be so brilliant in understanding the importance of structure and schedules. They did not want to rush her, so they agreed to remind her to come off in a few minutes.

Mama and Daddy were so proud of their brilliant daughter!

Once upon a time there was a small girl who really wanted to learn to dance. Every day she tried but no matter how much she tried, she just couldn't get the steps right.

The girl was very persistent. She touched her feet to the floor in the same way but she just couldn't do it correctly. She touched her knees and her hips, but the movements just weren't right. 

One day, she saw a dancer in the park. He was dancing with such grace and movement. The little girl just watched in amazement. 

The man saw the girl watching him and he stopped to see what she was doing. He touched her feet gently and said 'try these steps'. He touched her hands and her hips and showed her how to move them. She kept trying and trying, and eventually she was able to dance just like him! 

The little girl was so happy. She felt the happiness in her heart. From that day on she continued to practice and soon she was dancing like she had always dreamed!

name_of_work: How to Eat a Poem by Eve Merriam
content: Don't be polite. Bite in. Pick it up with your fingers and lick the juice that may run down your chin. It is ready and ripe now, whenever you are. You do not need a knife or fork or spoon or plate or napkin or tablecloth. For there is no core or stem or rind or pit or seed or skin to throw away.

Tom and Mia are friends. They like to play together. One day, they go to Mia's house for breakfast. Mia's mom makes toast for them. She puts butter and jam on the toast.

"Can I have some toast, please?" Tom asks.

"Sure, here you go," Mia's mom says. She gives Tom a plate with toast.

"Thank you," Tom says. He takes a bite of the toast. He makes a funny face. "This toast is funny," he says.

"What do you mean?" Mia asks. She looks at her toast. It looks normal to her.

"It tastes funny," Tom says. He shows Mia his tongue. It is purple.

Mia laughs. She sees the jam on Tom's toast. It is grape jam. "That's not funny, that's grape," she says. "Do you like grape?"

Tom thinks for a moment. He takes another bite of the toast. He smiles. "I do like grape," he says. "It is sweet and yummy."

Mia is happy. She likes grape too. She shares her toast with Tom. They eat all the toast. They say thank you to Mia's mom. They go to play with Mia's toys. They have a lot of fun. They are good friends.

Tim and Jen like to play in the park. They run, slide, swing and jump. They have a lot of fun. One day, they see a shiny thing on the grass. It is a razor. They do not know what it is.

Tim picks up the razor. He thinks it is a toy. He shows it to Jen. Jen wants to touch it too. She is careless. She grabs the razor from Tim. The razor is sharp. It cuts Jen's hand. Jen cries. She drops the razor.

Tim is scared. He sees blood on Jen's hand. He does not know what to do. He runs to find a grown-up. He sees a lady on a bench. He tells her what happened. The lady is kind. She takes Tim and Jen to a nurse. The nurse cleans Jen's hand and puts a band-aid on it. She tells them not to play with razors. They are not toys. They are dangerous.

Tim and Jen are sorry. They say thank you to the lady and the nurse. They learn a lesson. They promise to be careful next time. They hug each other. They go back to the park. They play with safe things. They still have fun.

Anna and Ben love to play with their toys. They have cars, dolls, blocks and a big elephant. The elephant is soft and gray and has a long nose. Anna and Ben like to hug the elephant and make it talk.

One day, Mom says it is time to go to the park. Anna and Ben are happy. They want to see the swings, the slide and the ducks. But Mom says they have to tidy their room first. She says they have to put their toys in the box and make their bed.

Anna and Ben do not want to tidy their room. They want to go to the park. They think Mom will not see their toys if they hide them under the bed. They rush to the bed and push their toys under it. All the toys except the elephant. The elephant is too big to fit under the bed.

Mom comes to check their room. She sees the bed is not made and the toys are under it. She is not happy. She says Anna and Ben have to tidy their room properly. She says they have to take out their toys and put them in the box. She says they have to make their bed and fluff their pillows. She says they have to say sorry to the elephant for leaving it out.

Anna and Ben feel bad. They love their elephant. They do not want to make it sad. They take out their toys and put them in the box. They make their bed and fluff their pillows. They hug the elephant and say sorry. They say they will not hide their toys again. They say they will be tidy.

Mom sees their room is tidy. She smiles. She says Anna and Ben are good children. She says they can go to the park now. She says they can take the elephant with them. Anna and Ben are happy. They take the elephant and go to the park. They have fun with the swings, the slide and the ducks. They share the elephant with their friends. The elephant is happy too.

Jimmy was a 3-year-old who loved to explore the beach. On this particular day, he had packed a bag with his shovel, bucket, and net and headed off to the shore.

When he arrived, he couldn't believe his eyes! Just a little ways ahead was a cute, gentle seal playing in the waves. Jimmy was mesmerized.

He slowly approached, wanting to get a better view. The seal stopped and looked at him, and Jimmy paused in surprise. The seal slowly moved closer, and Jimmy couldn't help but giggle.

The seal spoke to him, saying, "Hello Jimmy! I recommend you go this way today. It's a beautiful spot and I think you'll love it."

Jimmy was so excited! He thanked the seal and headed off, his heart filled with joy. After exploring the spot all morning, Jimmy returned to the beach, hoping the seal was still around. He was luckyâ€”there was the seal, playing in the waves.

Jimmy ran over, feeling so happy he'd made a new friend. He thanked the seal again and gave him a big hug before returning home. From that day forth, the seal was a part of Jimmyâ€™s adventures.

Once upon a time there was a family who loved each other very much. They ate dinner together every night and enjoyed delicious food. 

One night Dad had a great idea. Dad suggested that they could all go camping and explore the great outdoors. Everyone thought this was a brilliant suggestion and agreed to go.

The family packed up all their camping gear, loaded up the car, and drove out into the woods. They had the best time exploring nature, climbing hills, and looking for wildlife. 

At night they made a campfire and cooked a delicious dinner. They all sat around the fire, telling stories and snuggling up in blankets. It was a wonderful time. 

Back at home, the family looked back on the wonderful weekend with happiness. Dad suggested that they go camping once a month to enjoy the beauty of life together as a family. 

Everyone agreed wholeheartedly. They all knew that camping together was something delicious and special.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a doll that she loved to play with every day. One day, Lily's brother came into her room and saw the doll. He wanted to play with it too.

Lily said, "No, my doll!" Her brother replied, "Please, can I play with it too?" Lily thought for a moment and said, "Okay, but be careful with her."

Her brother took the doll and started to play. He made the doll open and close her eyes, and then he made her roar like a lion. Lily laughed and said, "That's silly!" They played together for a while, and then Lily's brother gave the doll back to her. They both had fun and were happy. The end.

name_of_work: Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part by Michael Drayton
content: Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part. Nay, I have done, you get no more of me; And I am glad, yea glad with all my heart, That thus so cleanly I myself can free. Shake hands for ever, cancel all our vows, And when we meet at any time again, Be it not seen in either of our brows That we one jot of former love retain. Now at the last gasp of Love's latest breath, When, his pulse failing, Passion speechless lies; When Faith is kneeling by his bed of death, And Innocence is closing up his eyes-- Now, if thou wouldst, when all have given him over, From death to life thou might'st him yet recover!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a big shelf in her room where she kept all her toys. One day, Lily found a little bird outside and she wanted to keep it as a pet. She gently picked up the bird and brought it to her room. 

Lily put the bird on the shelf with her other toys. She made sure to be gentle and not scare the bird. The bird felt safe and happy on the shelf with Lily's toys. 

Every day, Lily would visit the bird on the shelf and they would play together. The bird was happy to be kept as a pet by Lily. And Lily was happy to have a new friend on her shelf. The end.

name_of_work: A Toccata of Galuppi's by Robert Browning
content: I Oh Galuppi, Baldassaro, this is very sad to find! I can hardly misconceive you; it would prove me deaf and blind; But although I take your meaning, 'tis with such a heavy mind! II Here you come with your old music, and here's all the good it brings. What, they lived once thus at Venice where the merchants were the kings, Where Saint Mark's is, where the Doges used to wed the sea with rings? III Ay, because the sea's the street there; and 'tis arched by . . . what you call . . . Shylock's bridge with houses on it, where they kept the carnival: I was never out of England--it's as if I saw it all. IV Did young people take their pleasure when the sea was warm in May? Balls and masks begun at midnight, burning ever to mid-day, When they made up fresh adventures for the morrow, do you say? V Was a lady such a lady, cheeks so round and lips so red,-- On her neck the small face buoyant, like a bell-flower on its bed, O'er the breast's superb abundance where a man might base his head? VI Well, and it was graceful of them--they'd break talk off and afford --She, to bite her mask's black velvet--he, to finger on his sword, While you sat and played Toccatas, stately at the clavichord? VII What? Those lesser thirds so plaintive, sixths diminished, sigh on sigh, Told them something? Those suspensions, those solutions--"Must we die?" Those commiserating sevenths--"Life might last! we can but try! VIII "Were you happy?" --"Yes."--"And are you still as happy?"--"Yes. And you?" --"Then, more kisses!"--"Did I stop them, when a million seemed so few?" Hark, the dominant's persistence till it must be answered to! IX So, an octave struck the answer. Oh, they praised you, I dare say! "Brave Galuppi! that was music! good alike at grave and gay! "I can always leave off talking when I hear a master play!" X Then they left you for their pleasure: till in due time, one by one, Some with lives that came to nothing, some with deeds as well undone, Death stepped tacitly and took them where they never see the sun. XI But when I sit down to reason, think to take my stand nor swerve, While I triumph o'er a secret wrung from nature's close reserve, In you come with your cold music till I creep thro' every nerve. XII Yes, you, like a ghostly cricket, creaking where a house was burned: "Dust and ashes, dead and done with, Venice spent what Venice earned. "The soul, doubtless, is immortal--where a soul can be discerned. XIII "Yours for instance: you know physics, something of geology, "Mathematics are your pastime; souls shall rise in their degree; "Butterflies may dread extinction,--you'll not die, it cannot be! XIV "As for Venice and her people, merely born to bloom and drop, "Here on earth they bore their fruitage, mirth and folly were the crop: "What of soul was left, I wonder, when the kissing had to stop? XV "Dust and ashes!" So you creak it, and I want the heart to scold. Dear dead women, with such hair, too--what's become of all the gold Used to hang and brush their bosoms? I feel chilly and grown old.

Once upon a time, there was a helpful little bird named Blue. Blue lived in a big tree with many branches. He had lots of friends in the tree too.

One day, Blue saw a small bug stuck on a branch. The bug was sad and scared. Blue wanted to help the bug. So, he went to the branch and said, "Don't worry, I will help you."

Blue used his beak to gently pick up the bug. He put the bug down on a safe branch. The bug was very happy and said, "Thank you, Blue!" Blue felt good because he was helpful. From that day on, Blue always listened to his friends and helped them when they needed it.

Once upon a time, there was a pink sunflower. The sunflower lived in a big garden with many other flowers. Every day, the sunflower would look up at the sky and smile at the sun.

One day, something new happened. A little girl came to the garden. She saw the pink sunflower and said, "Wow! You are so pretty!" The sunflower felt very happy. The little girl would visit the sunflower every day and they became good friends.

The little girl and the pink sunflower played in the garden all summer long. They laughed and had fun together. When the wind blew, the sunflower would dance for the little girl. They were the best of friends and had the best time together.

Tom and Lily were playing in the living room with their toys. Tom had a new car that was very expensive. His dad gave it to him for his birthday. Lily had a doll that she loved very much. She got it from her mom.

"Can I play with your car, Tom?" Lily asked.

"No, it's mine. You can't touch it. It's too expensive. You might break it," Tom said.

"Please, Tom. Just for a little bit. I'll be careful. You can play with my doll," Lily said.

"No, no, no. Your doll is boring. Go away," Tom said.

Lily felt sad and angry. She wanted to play with the car. She thought Tom was mean. She waited until Tom was not looking. Then she grabbed the car and ran away. Tom saw her and shouted.

"Hey, give me back my car. That's not yours. That's stealing," Tom said.

He chased Lily around the house. Lily tried to hide, but Tom found her. He grabbed the car from her hands. He was very mad. He pushed Lily to the floor. Lily dropped her doll. The doll's head broke off.

Lily started to cry. She looked at her doll. She loved her doll. Now her doll was broken. She felt very bad.

"Look what you did. You broke my car. You scratched it. It's ruined. You're a bad sister. I hate you," Tom said.

He threw the car on the couch. He didn't care about it anymore. He went to his room and slammed the door.

Lily was still crying. She picked up her doll. She tried to put the head back on, but it didn't work. She hugged her doll. She wished Tom would say sorry. She wished he would forgive her. She wished they could play together again. But Tom didn't come out of his room. He didn't say anything. He didn't forgive her. He was still angry. Lily felt very lonely. She wished she had a nice brother. She wished she had a new doll. She wished she had never touched the car. But it was too late. She had made a big mistake. And she had to live with it. The end.

John was a generous young boy. His parents taught him the importance of being kind, so he tried his best to help others whenever he could.

One day, John went to the park. He saw an old man walking in without an umbrella. John offered the old man his umbrella, but he refused. John was about to leave when he noticed the old man was shivering. He had no coat on!

John gave him his coat. The old man was very thankful and he gave John a small note. He said, "This note will help you. Stay generous." John thanked him and the old man went away.

John opened the note and read it. The note said, "Your generosity will make you happy." From that day on, John tried his best to be generous whenever he could. He knew it made him happy, and it made other people happy too.

The south-wind strengthens to a gale, Across the moon the clouds fly fast, The house is smitten as with a flail, The chimney shudders to the blast. On such a night, when Air has loosed Its guardian grasp on blood and brain, Old terrors then of god or ghost Creep from their caves to life again; And Reason kens he herits in A haunted house. Tenants unknown Assert their squalid lease of sin With earlier title than his own. Unbodied presences, the pack'd Pollution and remorse of Time, Slipp'd from oblivion reenact The horrors of unhouseld crime. Some men would quell the thing with prayer Whose sightless footsteps pad the floor, Whose fearful trespass mounts the stair Or burts the lock'd forbidden door. Some have seen corpses long interr'd Escape from hallowing control, Pale charnel forms--nay ev'n have heard The shrilling of a troubled soul, That wanders till the dawn hath cross'd The dolorous dark, or Earth hath wound Closer her storm-spredd cloke, and thrust The baleful phantoms underground.

Once upon a time there were two friends. One friend was called Bob and the other was called Sam. They both liked to do trades. They would trade their favourite toys with each other.

Once, Bob had a brilliant idea. He suggested they should do a big trade. They spent the whole day collecting the things they wanted to trade. Then when they had everything ready they sat down together to do the trade.

Sam was very happy with what he got from Bob. He said it was brilliant. Bob was also very happy with what he got from Sam. They both thanked each other for doing the trade.

Now whenever Bob and Sam want something new to play with, they do a trade. They always remember the big trade they did together and it makes them very happy.

name_of_work: To the Boys Who May One Day Date My Daughter by Jesse Parent
content: To the boys who may one day date my daughter! I have been waiting for you. Since before her birth, Since before my spark took hold and ignited the fire in her mother's belly, I have been training to kill you. When you took your first steps I was preparing to make it so you never walked again, When you played at war I was perfecting headshots, You can't catch up at this point. And when you first meet my daughter and fall in love with the look she sends over her shoulder, Her crescent-moon eyes framing her laughing smile, you Are gonna wanna talk to her. And when those hours pass by like sprinters during that first timeless conversation- You will also know with a deep and impending sense of dread, That you are going to have to talk to me When you first come to my home, and see the bone carving over my threshold- Try not to imagine your own femurs so expertly carved. Pay no attention to my "ample crawl space", my "Room with a rubber mat and a drain", be careful To only approach me with love for my daughter, See, I have been seeding her childhood with tap-root hugs To weed out indifference and apathy, There will be no Daddy Issues for your teenage talons to latch upon. If you Break her heart; I will hear it snap with the ear I pressed against her mother's belly- The elbow I cradled her head in will send a message to my fist. My cheeks Are attuned to her lips. I will know if they tremble. I have taught her that a man should never hit a woman- Now her mother would like to add that you really shouldn't ever hit anybody- But I have taught her that a man should never hit a woman. Consider my genes a mark of Cain; You will suffer seven times whatever you do to her, And she will not keep your secret: You can't make fire feel afraid. I have been teaching her love all of her life, And all that I ask is that you continue the lesson. Love her. Befriend her. Protect her- be there when I can't, and when my body gives up to the grave, Let the grin that eternity carves into my face be a reflection of the peace that your love brings to her, And we should get along just fine... ADDENDUM: To the girls who may one day date my daughter!... My wife is a better shot than I am.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She lived in a big house with her mommy and daddy. One day, Lily was playing outside with her toys when she saw a big tornado in the sky. 

Lily ran inside to tell her mommy and daddy. "Mommy, Daddy, look outside! There's a big tornado!" she said. 

Her mommy and daddy looked outside and saw the tornado too. "We need to go to the basement, it's not safe upstairs," said her daddy. 

Lily and her family went to the basement and waited for the tornado to pass. After a while, they went back upstairs to see if everything was okay. "Phew, that was a busy tornado," said Lily's mommy. "But we're all okay and that's what matters." 

Lily was happy that her family was safe and that they all owned their big house together.

name_of_work: The New Bride by Catherine Smith
content: Dying, darling, is the easy bit. Fifty paracetamol, bride-white and sticking in the throat, ten shots of Johnny Walker, and the deed is done. A twilight day of drowsing, then the breathing slows to a whisper, like a sinner in Confession. Death is dead easy. No, what happens next is the difficulty. You bastard, howlng in public, snivelling over photos, ringing round for consolation. And you have me burnt, like a dinner gone wrong, you keep the charred remains of me on show at the Wake, inviting everyone I hate. Oh God, they come in packs, sleek as rats with platitudes and an eye on my half of the bed, hoping to find leftover skin, a hint of fetid breath. I leave them no hairs on the pillow. There are none to leave. And a year to the day since I shrug off the yoke of life, you meet the new bride. In group therapy. You head straight for a weeper and wailer, telling strangers all her little tragedies. You love the way she languishes, her tears sliming your neck, you give in to her on vile pink Austrian blinds. The Wedding is a riot of white nylon. Everybody drinks your health and hers, the simpering bitch. She and Della Smith keep you fat and happy as a pig in shit. I want her cells to go berserk. Some nights I slip between you. The new bride sleeps buttoned up, slug-smug in polyester. You, my faithless husband, turn over in your dreams, and I'm there, ice-cold and seeking out your eyes and for a moment you brush my lips, and freeze.

Once upon a time there lived Noreen, a brave little girl who lived all alone in a tiny house in the countryside. She was very lonely and wished she had someone to help her out, like a best friend. 

One day, Noreen heard a soft voice coming from outside. She looked out the window and saw a butterfly perched on a tree branch. 

"Who are you?" asked Noreen.

"I'm a special butterfly!" said the butterfly in a musical voice. "My name is Jenny and I'm here to help you find a special treasure!"

Noreen was so excited! She and Jenny set off into the forest, searching for the treasure all day. Finally, after a long journey, they reached the top of a hill with a small cave at its centre. 

"This is it!" said Jenny. "Let's say a prayer before we go in to find the treasure."

The two said a short prayer and then entered the cave. Inside, they found the treasure they'd been searching for all day. Noreen was so happy. She hugged Jenny and thanked her for helping her find her special treasure.

And that is how Noreen and Jenny became best friends - all thanks to a special treasure and a simple prayer.

Once there was a little girl named Susie who loved butterflies. One day she was walking in the garden and she saw a broken butterfly. She gently picked it up and started to cry, because memories of her own broken wings came flooding back. She remembered how it felt when she was younger and didn't know how to fly.

Her mom saw her crying and came to hug her. She said, "Susie, why are you crying?"

"Mom, I don't know how to help this hurt butterfly," Susie said.

"Sometimes, even if we have broken wings, we still have the power to help others fly," her mom said.

So Susie tried her best to fix the broken wings of the butterfly and, with patience and love, she succeeded. That day Susie learned that even if we have been broken, we can still be a light for others and help them.

Tom and Jen are twins. They like to play with their toys in their room. But sometimes they fight over the toys. One day, they find a box of matches in their dad's drawer. They think the matches are fun and shiny.

"Let me have a match!" Tom says. He grabs a match from the box.

"No, it's mine!" Jen says. She pulls the match from Tom's hand.

They tug and pull the match until it breaks in two. They both cry.

"Look what you did!" Tom says. He throws his half of the match on the floor.

"Your fault!" Jen says. She rubs her half of the match on the wall.

The match makes a spark and a flame. The flame is fierce and hot. It burns the wall and the curtain.

"Fire! Fire!" Tom and Jen scream. They run out of the room.

Their mom and dad hear them and smell the smoke. They rush to the room and see the fire. They use water and a blanket to put out the fire.

They are angry and scared. They hug Tom and Jen and tell them to never play with matches again.

"Matches are not toys. Matches are dangerous. Matches can hurt you and the house," their mom says.

"We're sorry, mom. We're sorry, dad. We didn't know. We won't do it again," Tom and Jen say.

They are sorry and sad. They learn a lesson. They promise to share their toys and not fight. They also promise to not touch matches ever again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Emmy. She was so excited that it was a thunderstorm day! She had heard from her parents that lightning was very special.

When the lightning happened, Emmy watched outside the window and saw the most amazing sight. The sky was lit up with a colorful lightshow! The lightning made patterns of bright yellows, purples and reds.

Emmy shouted for joy and jumped around. She was so very excited. She laughed and laughed at the lightning and the colorful sky.

Suddenly, the thunderstorm was over. The sky was quiet and the lightning was gone. But Emmy still felt excited because of all the wonderful lightning she had seen.

Once upon a time, there was a red car named Max. Max loved to drive fast and do loops around the track. One day, Max met a lion named Leo. Leo liked to roar very loudly. 

"Hi Leo," said Max. "Why do you like to roar so much?"

"I roar to show everyone that I am big and strong," replied Leo.

Max thought for a moment and then said, "I like to do loops to show everyone that I am fast and brave."

Leo smiled and said, "We are both very good at something. Let's be friends and show everyone what we can do together!"

Max and Leo became best friends and would often do loops and roar together. They were very happy and everyone could see that they were the best of friends.

The sun was shining brightly in the sky. Mary was very excited, for she had a new blouse given by her mum. Mary's friends were all envious of the new blouse. But just as she was about to show her friends her blouse, it started to rain. Mary was very disappointed, her new blouse was getting wet. She hoped it will dry soon.

But the rain didn't stop. As the rain got harder and harder, Mary quickly ran home. When she reached home, she saw her blouse was all wet. She sadly hung it on the wall to dry.

The next day, Mary was excited to wear her new blouse again. But to her surprise, it was all stained. The rain ruined her blouse and it was no longer shine when she looked at it.

Mary was so sad, she wished the rain did not come. She wanted her new blouse to shine again. Unfortunately, that did not happen, and her blouse never shone again.

name_of_work: Spring and All by William Carlos Williams
content: By the road to the contagious hospital under the surge of the blue mottled clouds driven from the northeast-a cold wind. Beyond, the waste of broad, muddy fields brown with dried weeds, standing and fallen patches of standing water the scattering of tall trees All along the road the reddish purplish, forked, upstanding, twiggy stuff of bushes and small trees with dead, brown leaves under them leafless vines-- Lifeless in appearance, sluggish dazed spring approaches-- They enter the new world naked, cold, uncertain of all save that they enter. All about them the cold, familiar wind-- Now the grass, tomorrow the stiff curl of wildcarrot leaf One by one objects are defined-- It quickens: clarity, outline of leaf But now the stark dignity of entrance--Still, the profound change has come upon them: rooted, they grip down and begin to awaken

Once upon a time there was a pink valley. It was filled with trees, birds, and many shiny things that glowed in the sun. There were animals running around and playing as the wind softly blew.

One day, a little girl walked into the valley. She had a basket filled with apples. As she looked around, she heard a voice call out, "Keep those apples, little girl!"

She looked around but didn't see anyone. Then she heard the voice again, but this time it came from a big furry bear. The bear was standing in front of her and said, "I'm the guardian of this valley. Please keep those apples, so all the animals can enjoy them!"

The little girl smiled and said, "I will keep them, bear!" She carefully divided the apples among the animals, and they all seemed very happy.

The bear nodded with satisfaction and said, "You have been a good friend, little girl. Keep the valley pink!"

The little girl nodded and said, "I will keep it pink!"

And so she did. Every time she came back to the valley, it was as pink and happy as ever.

Once upon a time there was a princess. She liked to play outside in the rain. One day it started to rain. She wanted to keep playing, so she ran and ran until she was soaking wet. All of a sudden, the rain stopped and it got very cold. She shivered and wished it was warm again. 

The princess heard a noise in the sky. She looked up and saw a big cloud in the sky. The princess was scared and ran home until she was safe inside. 

The next morning, the princess woke up and looked outside. Everything was covered in white. The snow had frozen the ground like a sheet of ice. The princess was amazed and went outside to play in the snow. She laughed and made snowballs. She was so excited!

But then, she heard a noise in the sky. She looked up and saw the big cloud again. It was cold, snow began to fall and it was very dark. The princess ran to her home and quickly ran inside. 

Outside, the snow kept falling and the temperature became colder and colder. Suddenly, everything froze! The garden trees, flowers, everything had frozen solid. The princess was so happy the next morning when the sun melted the ice. She enjoyed playing in the warm sun and rain again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. Sue had a big, round head. One day, Sue felt troubled. She did not know what to do.

Sue went to her mom and said, "Mom, I am troubled. Can you help me?" Her mom said, "Let's sit down and talk." So, they sat down and talked about what was troubling Sue. Sue told her mom that she was sad because her head was big and round.

Her mom hugged her and said, "Sue, your big, round head is what makes you special. It is a part of who you are. Let's be happy and love our big, round heads." Sue smiled and felt better. From that day on, Sue was not troubled about her big, round head. She was happy and loved herself just the way she was.

Once upon a time, there was a bossy cat named Mittens. Mittens liked to tell everyone what to do. She meowed loudly and always wanted things her way. One day, Mittens saw a little mouse scurrying by. She thought to herself, "I want to catch that mouse!"

Mittens waited patiently for the mouse to come closer. She pounced, but the mouse was too quick and ran away. Mittens was disappointed. She tried again and again, but the mouse always got away.

One day, Mittens saw the mouse again. This time, she didn't try to catch it. Instead, she meowed softly and said, "Hello little mouse. Do you want to be friends?" The mouse was surprised but happy to have a new friend. Mittens learned that being bossy doesn't always work, and sometimes it's better to be kind.

One day, there was a curious boy. He was playing outside with his golf ball. He took a swing and hit the ball. It traveled so far, it went into a garden. 

The boy was excited and he ran to the garden to get his golf ball. He looked around but he couldn't find it. The boy looked very high and very low but still couldn't find the golf ball. 

Then he heard a voice, â€œWhy are you here?â€ Startled, he looked around and saw a lady.

The boy said, â€œI hit the golf ball very far, but now I can't find it.â€ The lady smiled and said, â€œFollow me, I know where it is.â€

The boy was happy and followed the lady to a tree, and there was his lost golf ball! 

The lady gave the boy the golf ball and said, â€œThat was a very good strike!â€ The boy beamed and thanked the lady for finding his golf ball.

One day, John was in his kitchen counting his five apples. He had three green ones and two pink ones. They looked so healthy, he could not wait to eat them.

Suddenly, a big monster appeared in front of him! The monster said in a deep voice, "give me the pink apples!". John was so scared. He picked up the two pink apples and slowly handed them over to the monster. 

John asked, "please don't take them, they are so healthy and I still haven't eaten them". But the monster didn't care. It just snatched the apples away and said, "these apples belong to me now!"

Unfortunately, there was nothing John could do. The monster was too big and strong. He sadly watched as the monster disappeared with his two pink apples.

One day, a little boy named Tim went for a walk. He wore his favorite navy hat. As he stepped outside, he saw a big, loud dog. The dog barked at Tim. Tim felt scared.

Tim's friend, Sam, came to help. Sam said, "Don't worry, Tim. I will talk to the dog." Sam walked up to the dog and said, "Please don't be loud. You are scaring my friend." The dog stopped barking and wagged its tail.

Tim felt happy and said, "Thank you, Sam." They learned that talking to someone can solve a problem. From that day on, Tim and Sam were not scared of the big, loud dog. They became friends with the dog and played together every day.

Once upon a time, there was a poor family who lived in a small house. The house was not big, but it was cozy and warm. The family had a little girl named Lily. Lily loved to sing and dance, and she always sang the same song over and over again.

One day, Lily's mother asked her to repeat the song again. Lily smiled and sang her song again. Her mother was happy and clapped her hands. Lily felt proud of herself. 

Every day, Lily would sing her song in the house. Her family loved to hear her sing. They would dance and sing along with her. Even though they were poor, they were happy because they had each other and Lily's beautiful voice.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside in the mud. He would jump and stomp in it, making a big mess. 

One day, Timmy's mom told him that he needed to clean up the mud before he could go inside. Timmy didn't want to clean up, he just wanted to play. So he left the mud on his clothes and went inside anyway. 

Later that day, Timmy's mom took him to the store. They walked down the toy aisle and Timmy saw a great toy he wanted. But his mom said no because he didn't clean up the mud. Timmy felt sad and realized that he should have listened to his mom. From then on, he always cleaned up his messes before doing anything else.

Every morning the world is created. Under the orange sticks of the sun the heaped ashes of the night turn into leaves again and fasten themselves to the high branches- and the ponds appear like black cloth on which are painted islands of summer lilies. If it is your nature to be happy you will swim away along the soft trails for hours, your imagination alighting everywhere. And if your spirit carries within it the thorn that is heavier than lead- if it's all you can do to keep on trudging- there is still somewhere deep within you a beast shouting that the earth is exactly what it wanted- each pond with its blazing lilies is a prayer heard and answered lavishly, every morning, whether or not you have ever dared to be happy, whether or not you have ever dared to pray.

Once upon a time, there were two friends, Max and Ben. They were playing in the garden, when they saw the big gate. Max said to Ben, "Let's come to the gate!" Ben was excited and they ran together to the gate.

Once they reached the gate, they saw it was closed. Max said to Ben, "I'm gonna push it!" Ben said, "That's a stupid plan!" But Max kept trying. He kept pushing and pushing, but the gate wouldn't move.

After a few minutes of trying, Max said to Ben, "I'm tired of pushing. I don't think we can open the gate." 

Ben said, "Come, let's look around for something else to do." 

So Max and Ben went away from the gate, and had lots of fun in the garden instead.

Once upon a time, there was a mommy who liked to cook. She wore an apron to keep her clothes clean. One day, she was making pancakes for breakfast when she accidentally spilled some batter on the floor. Her little girl saw what happened and wanted to help. She got a towel to support her mommy and clean up the terrible mess. Mommy was so happy and gave her a big hug. From that day on, the little girl always helped her mommy in the kitchen, wearing her own tiny apron.

Once upon a time, there was a big, friendly dog named Max. Max loved to play fetch and go for walks with his owner, Emily. One day, Max and Emily went to the park to play. Max chased after the ball and brought it back to Emily.

Suddenly, a boy came over and said that he didn't like dogs. Emily asked him why and he said it was just his opinion. Max didn't like that and began to bark and yell at the boy. Emily told Max to calm down and that everyone has their own opinion.

After playing for a while longer, Emily and Max went home. Emily told Max that he was a brilliant dog and gave him a treat. Max wagged his tail happily and went to sleep, dreaming of playing fetch again the next day.

THERE'S no use in weeping, Though we are condemned to part: There's such a thing as keeping A remembrance in one's heart: There's such a thing as dwelling On the thought ourselves have nurs'd, And with scorn and courage telling The world to do its worst. We'll not let its follies grieve us, We'll just take them as they come; And then every day will leave us A merry laugh for home. When we've left each friend and brother, When we're parted wide and far, We will think of one another, As even better than we are. Every glorious sight above us, Every pleasant sight beneath, We'll connect with those that love us, Whom we truly love till death ! In the evening, when we're sitting By the fire perchance alone, Then shall heart with warm heart meeting, Give responsive tone for tone. We can burst the bonds which chain us, Which cold human hands have wrought, And where none shall dare restrain us We can meet again, in thought. So there's no use in weeping, Bear a cheerful spirit still; Never doubt that Fate is keeping Future good for present ill !

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to watch films with his mommy and daddy. One day, Timmy and his family went to see a film at the movie theater. The film was about a big, fearful monster who lived in a castle. 

Timmy loved the movie, but he was scared of the monster. His mommy and daddy told him that the monster was just acting, and that it wasn't real. Timmy felt better knowing that the monster wasn't real, and he enjoyed the rest of the film. 

After the film was over, Timmy and his family went home. Timmy couldn't stop talking about the film and how the monster was just acting. He wanted to watch more films with his family, and he wasn't afraid of any monsters anymore.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to eat sausages for breakfast. One day, Timmy's mom made him a delicious sausage for breakfast. Timmy admired the sausage and said, "Mom, this sausage is really yummy!"

After breakfast, Timmy went to play with his toys. He was playing with his favorite toy car when his little sister came into the room crying. Timmy asked, "What's wrong, sis?" His sister said, "I lost my teddy bear and I can't find it anywhere!" Timmy remained calm and said, "Don't worry, I'll help you find it." 

Timmy and his sister searched the whole house and finally found the teddy bear under the bed. Timmy's sister was so happy and said, "Thank you, Timmy! You're the best brother ever!" Timmy smiled and said, "I just wanted to help. That's what big brothers do."

Tom and Lily were playing in the garden. They liked to run and jump and laugh. They saw a big bird in the sky. It was black and white and had a long tail. It was a magpie.

"Look, Lily, a magpie!" Tom said. "It can soar very high. Do you think it can see us?"

Lily nodded. She liked magpies. They were shiny and smart. She wanted to talk to it. She waved her hand and shouted, "Hello, magpie! Do you want to play with us?"

The magpie heard Lily. It was curious and jolly. It flew down and landed on the hedge. It tilted its head and said, "Hello, children! I can play with you. What do you want to do?"

Tom and Lily were happy. They had a new friend. They asked the magpie to show them how it could soar. The magpie agreed. It flapped its wings and soared up and down and around. It made funny noises and tricks. Tom and Lily clapped and cheered. They had a lot of fun with the magpie. They played until the sun set. Then they said goodbye and thanked the magpie for playing with them. The magpie said goodbye and soared away. Tom and Lily went inside and told their mum and dad about their adventure. They hoped to see the magpie again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play at the park with her friends. They would run and jump and laugh together. One day, they saw a big slide and they all wanted to go on it.

Lily climbed up the ladder and slid down the slide. It was so much fun! But then, she saw a post at the bottom of the slide. She tried to stop herself, but she couldn't and she hit the post. It hurt a lot and she felt very uncomfortable.

Her friends tried to help her, but she was too hurt to play anymore. She had to go to the hospital and get a cast on her arm. Lily was very sad that she couldn't play with her friends for a long time. She learned to be more careful when playing at the park.

name_of_work: The Falling Leaves by Margaret Postgate Cole
content: Today, as I rode by, I saw the brown leaves dropping from their tree In a still afternoon, When no wind whirled them whistling to the sky, But thickly, silently, They fell, like snowflakes wiping out the noon; And wandered slowly thence For thinking of a gallant multitude Which now all withering lay, Slain by no wind of age or pestilence, But in their beauty strewed Like snowflakes falling on the Flemish clay.

Once upon a time, there was a plastic toy boat. It lived on the beach, and it was very adventurous. Every day the boat would go on the water and explore, searching for new things.

One day the boat got too daring, and decided to go very far from the beach. It was so far away, it couldn't get back. It was stuck, and no one was there to take care of it.

The boat started to miss the beach, and all the fun it had there. It stayed for a very long time, but no one ever found it. It was sad and alone, and the boat wished it had been a bit less adventurous. 

Alas, the boat never made it back to the beach. Its story is a reminder to always take care while exploring.

name_of_work: A Ballad of Two Knights by Sara Teasdale
content: Two knights rode forth at early dawn A-seeking maids to wed, Said one, "My lady must be fair, With gold hair on her head." Then spake the other knight-at-arms: "I care not for her face, But she I love must be a dove For purity and grace." And each knight blew upon his horn And went his separate way, And each knight found a lady-love Before the fall of day. But she was brown who should have had The shining yellow hair, I ween the knights forgot their words Or else they ceased to care. For he who wanted purity Brought home a wanton wild, And when each saw the other knight I seen that each knight smiled.

Maggie was three years old and she loved to play with her cards. One day, Maggie was playing a card game with her daddy. She put the cards in a pile and then held one in each hand. She was about to put the cards in the pile when she heard her daddy say "Wait, let me show you something much easier". 

Maggie looked at her daddy and asked "What can I do?". Her daddy leaned over and said "It's easy. Just put one card on top of the other card like this". He demonstrated by slowly leaning one card over the other card until they were touching. 

Maggie smiled, eager to try it herself. She picked up two cards and leaned one over the other. "I did it!" she exclaimed. 

Maggie's daddy smiled. "That was easy, wasn't it?" he said. Maggie nodded enthusiastically, and they continued to play the card game.

name_of_work: Imagining Their Own Hymns by Brigit Pegeen Kelly
content: What fools they are to believe the angels in this window are in ecstasy. They do not smile. Their eyes are rolled back in annoyance not in bliss, as my mother's eyes roll back when she finds us in the dirt with the cider-- flies and juice blackening our faces and hands. When the sun comes up behind the angels then even in their dun robes they are beautiful, with their girlish hair and their mean lit faces, but they do not love the light. As I do not love it when I am made clean for the ladies who bring my family money. They stroke my face and smooth my hair. So sweet, they say, so good, but I am not sweet or good. I would take one of the possums we kill in the dump by the woods where the rats slide like dark boats into the dark stream and leave it on the heavy woman's porch just to think of her on her knees scrubbing and scrubbing at a stain that will never come out. And these angels that the women turn to are not good either. They are sick of Jesus, who never stops dying, hanging there white and large, his shadow blue as pitch, and blue the bruise on his chest, with spread petals, like the hydrangea blooms I tear from Mrs. Macht's bush and smash on the sidewalk. One night they will get out of here. One night when the weather is turning cold and a few candles burn, they will leave St. Blase standing under his canopy of glass lettuce and together, as in a wedding march, their pockets full of money from the boxes for the sick poor, they will walk down the aisle, imagining their own hymns, past the pews and the water fonts in which small things float, down the streets of our narrow town, while the bells ring and the birds fly up in the fields beyond--and they will never come back.

Lily and Max were playing in the garden. They saw a big bug with many legs and a hard shell. It was dull and brown, not pretty like a butterfly or a ladybug.

"Look, a bug!" Lily said. "Let's catch it and put it in a jar."

Max nodded. He ran to get a jar and a lid. Lily followed him with the bug in her hand. They put the bug in the jar and closed the lid. They felt happy and proud.

They showed the jar to their mom. She was not happy. She looked at the bug and frowned.

"Why did you catch the bug?" she asked. "Don't you know that bugs need air and space to live?"

Lily and Max felt sorry. They did not think about that. They thought the bug was just a toy.

"Can we keep it, mom?" Max asked. "We will give it some leaves and water."

Mom shook her head. "No, you can't keep it. The bug is not happy in the jar. It is scared and sad. You have to let it go. How would you feel if someone put you in a jar and covered you with a lid?"

Lily and Max imagined being in a jar. They felt scared and sad too. They did not want that.

"OK, mom. We will let it go." Lily said. "We are sorry, bug. We did not mean to hurt you."

They opened the jar and let the bug out. The bug crawled away quickly. It looked happier and freer.

Lily and Max learned a lesson. They learned that bugs are not toys. They learned to respect and care for all living things. They learned to be kind and gentle.

Once upon a time there was a very thin voice. It was so thin it was almost whispering.
Every day the voice sounded all over the town.
One day everyone started to act a little different. They smiled more, and started to do nice things for each other.

The townspeople soon discovered where the thin voice was coming from. It was coming from a little bird.
The bird would tweet beautiful songs every day and whenever it sang, the townspeople would act nice.

The townspeople were so happy they gave the bird a special nest in the biggest tree of the town. In return, the bird sang extra loud.

From that day on life in the town was always happy and peaceful, all thanks to the little bird's thin voice.
